chunks.text:
See TAIL OS run on a Linux machine with QEMU — no board, no toolchain, no build. Every
command from step 2 on was run against the published image with QEMU 10.2, and the output
shown is what it printed.

You need a Linux machine with at least 2 CPUs and enough free disk for QEMU and TAIL OS. On
Ubuntu 24.04 the QEMU packages below take 580 to 970 MiB, depending on what is already
installed; TAIL OS takes about 300 MiB more, or about 600 MiB if you also follow
[Without the launcher](#without-the-launcher), which keeps its own copy.

QEMU emulates the Raspberry Pi 3's four CPU cores. It runs best with 4 or more CPUs (`nproc`
counts them) and more slowly with 2. With 1 it is slower still: on our machine the shell came
up in about 13 seconds and `python /hello.py` took about 18, and timings vary from run to run.

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils
```

Download the launcher, then run it:

```bash
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/run_tailos_qemu.sh
chmod +x run_tailos_qemu.sh
./run_tailos_qemu.sh
```

The launcher downloads the kernel and data disk into `~/.cache/tailos/`, checks each
against the published `SHA256SUMS`, and boots them. The first run downloads about 15 MiB,
which unpacks to about 263 MiB in the cache. It shows no progress while it does: after
`fetching https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_disk.img.gz` nothing more appears until the
download, unpacking and check are done. Later runs start from the cache, which the launcher
replaces only when a new image is published, so booting again is just `./run_tailos_qemu.sh`.
Each run still fetches the small `SHA256SUMS` to check for a new image, so it needs the
network.

Boot takes a few seconds: about 1 on our machine, with 4 CPUs and QEMU 10.2, and about 8 on
a 2-CPU cloud machine with Ubuntu 24.04's QEMU 8.2. A slower machine takes longer, and the log can pause for a while, longest just before the line ending
`FAT File System Server initialized`, but it has not hung.

Before the shell starts, the launcher prints a few lines of its own, then TAIL OS prints a banner
beginning `TailOS  aarch64 / rpi3  build` and about 40 lines of boot log, each tagged `[STRT]`,
`[ OK ]` or `[INFO]`. The two `[INFO]` lines where the wifi and bt expander
`did not acknowledge` are expected: QEMU's emulated firmware ignores that request. Lines
from different services can arrive out of timestamp order. When the shell starts you see:

```
TAIL OS Shell (tsh)
Type 'exit' to quit, 'help' for built-in commands.

/$
```

To leave QEMU at any point, press **Ctrl-A**, then a lowercase **x**. QEMU prints `QEMU: Terminated`
and you are back at your own shell.

Each command below answers within a second or two, and `python /hello.py` within several
seconds. Wait for the `/$` prompt before typing the next command; text typed while a command
is still running appears twice.

```
/$ help
Built-in commands:
  exit [code]    - Exit the shell (optionally with exit code)
  cd [dir]       - Change current working directory
  pwd            - Print current working directory
  echo [-n] args - Print arguments ($VAR expanded)
  export K=V     - Set (and export) an environment variable
  cat <file...>  - Display file contents
  clear          - Clear the terminal screen
  history        - Show command history
  mkdir <dir...> - Create directories
  touch <file..> - Create empty files
  test EXPR      - Evaluate a conditional expression
  [ EXPR ]       - Same as 'test', with a closing ']'
  true / false   - Yield success / failure status
  help           - Show this help message

Scripting: 'tsh <file> [args]' runs a script; if/while/for, &&, ||,
';', $?, $1..$@ and '#!/rfs/tsh' shebangs are supported.

External commands are executed as separate processes.
```

```
/$ ls /
etc       hello.py  usr
/$ ls /usr/bin
bluetoothctl    isrfat          netstat         route           waitfor
cp              kill            ping            shutdown        wcetdump
dhcp            list-root-long  ps              sleep           which
fetch           logview         python          time            wifi
find            ls              reboot          top
grep            mv              rm              vi
```

```
/$ ps
PID    PPID   STATE      THREADS  NAME
0      -      LOADING    0        startup
1      -      RUNNING    11       kernel
2      -      RUNNING    2        uart_pl011
3      -      RUNNING    3        log_server
4      -      RUNNING    1        pipe_server
5      -      RUNNING    2        dwc2_rpi3
6      -      RUNNING    4        network
8      -      RUNNING    5        gpio_rpi3
9      -      RUNNING    1        sd_sdhost_rpi3
10     -      RUNNING    1        read_only_file_system_server
11     -      RUNNING    1        fat_file_system_server
13     -      RUNNING    1        tsh
14     13     RUNNING    1        ps
```

This is what a microkernel looks like from the inside. The serial driver, the USB and SD
card drivers, both filesystems and the network stack are not part of `kernel`; each is a
process of its own, listed here beside the shell.

```
/$ python /hello.py
hello from tailos
```

`python` prints nothing for several seconds before its line. The first run after boot is the
slow one: about 4 seconds on our 4-CPU machine with QEMU 10.2, and about 17 on the 2-CPU
cloud machine with QEMU 8.2. It has not hung. Run it again and it takes under a second on
our machine and about 4 seconds on the cloud machine.

```
/$ ping -c 3 10.0.2.2
PING 10.0.2.2 (10.0.2.2)
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=0 time=7.199 ms
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=1 time=3.441 ms
reply from 10.0.2.2: seq=2 time=2.982 ms
--- 10.0.2.2 statistics ---
3 sent, 3 received, 0% lost
```

`10.0.2.2` is QEMU's gateway on the emulated network. The replies travel through the
guest's USB network device, its driver and the `network` process above. The times differ
on every run. With 2 CPUs a reply can miss ping's 1-second timeout: that probe prints
`no reply: seq=N`, and the last line counts it as lost.

If you would rather not run a script, the same steps by hand. Run them in an empty
directory: they keep no cache, the files land there, `gunzip` stops and asks before
replacing files an earlier run left behind, and it unpacks the disk image to 256 MiB.

```bash
mkdir tailos-manual && cd tailos-manual
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_qemu.rfs.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_disk.img.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
gunzip tail_qemu.rfs.gz tail_disk.img.gz
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

qemu-system-aarch64 \
    -M raspi3b \
    -kernel tail_qemu.rfs \
    -serial mon:stdio \
    -display none \
    -drive file=tail_disk.img,format=raw,if=sd \
    -netdev user,id=tailnet0 \
    -device usb-net,netdev=tailnet0
```

`-M raspi3b` emulates a Raspberry Pi 3B. The last two flags give the guest a USB network
device behind QEMU's user-mode networking, which needs no special permissions on your
machine; without them the guest boots with no network.

- [Periodic framework — Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md):
  write a node that runs on a fixed period.
- [Periodic framework — Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md):
  the same, in Python.

The SDK is what you build TAIL OS applications with: the portable OS and the
toolchain that targets it. It needs no TAIL OS source and no cross-compiler —
the bundled toolchain links with its own `rust-lld`.

TAIL OS ships as two artifacts. The SDK here is **board-agnostic**: install it
once and the same install serves every board. A **bootable image** for a
specific board is built from a separate per-board BSP against this SDK. The
Raspberry Pi 3 BSP is a download too: see
[Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](install_rpi3.md).

To try TAIL OS without installing anything, see the [Quick Start](quick_start_public.md):
it boots a prebuilt image in QEMU with one script.

| | |
|---|---|
| Linux on x86-64 | The bundled toolchain runs there |
| `rustup` | The installer registers the bundled toolchain with it: [rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs) |
| `curl` and `tar` | Usually preinstalled |

QEMU is needed only to boot an image, not to build applications:
`sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils`.

```bash
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0.tar.gz
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
```

The bundle is 289 MiB: it carries the toolchain and the portable OS, so nothing
is fetched during installation.

```bash
tar xzf tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0.tar.gz
cd tail-sdk-installer-0.1.0
./install.sh --prefix ~/tail-sdk
```

`install.sh` copies the toolchain and the portable OS into the directory you
name, registers the toolchain with rustup as `tail_release` pointing there, and
writes `~/tail-sdk/tail-sdk-env.sh`, which exports `TAIL_SDK` (the SDK tree
inside the install, `~/tail-sdk/sdk/tail-sdk-0.1.0`). It finishes by
compiling and linking a throwaway program, so a successful run means the next
step works. The extracted bundle is disposable afterwards.

Run it without `--prefix` to be prompted for the directory, with `--profile` to
add the env file to your shell startup, and with `--force` to reinstall over an
existing install.

```bash
cargo +tail_release new my_app && cd my_app
cargo +tail_release build --target aarch64-unknown-tail
```

That produces an AArch64 ELF for TAIL OS with no further configuration. The
`+tail_release` selects the installed toolchain; `rustup default tail_release`
makes a bare `cargo build` use it.

Application builds need nothing else. `TAIL_SDK` matters only when building a
board BSP, whose `verify-sdk.sh` reads it:

```bash
source ~/tail-sdk/tail-sdk-env.sh
```

- [Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](install_rpi3.md): download the BSP,
  `bsp-rpi3.zip`, and build an SD card image against this SDK. Programs that use
  the periodic framework are built there too.
- [The periodic framework in Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md)
  and [in Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md): the API
  for periodic applications, with examples.
- [Quick Start](quick_start_public.md): boot a prebuilt image in QEMU.
- [Running TAIL OS in QEMU](install_qemu.md).

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
TailOS is a microkernel real-time operating system for robots. User programs get the full
Rust standard library, and Python runs on the same framework. A robot application is a set
of small programs: **nodes** that run on a fixed period and exchange data on **topics**,
and **services** that answer requests. This page names the pieces and shows where each
one runs. The guides linked at the end show how to write them.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: What runs where in a TailOS robot application accDescr: Periodic nodes, aperiodic services, device drivers, servers and shell tools are each separate user-space processes. Nodes reach the microkernel through topics and services through requests; the drivers, servers and tools also run on the microkernel, which provides threads, scheduling, memory, IPC and topics. subgraph USER["user space"] NODE("periodic nodes
sensor, estimator, controller"):::prog SVC{{"aperiodic services
request and reply"}}:::svc DRV[/"device drivers
GPIO, I2C, PWM, stepper"\]:::hw SRV{{"servers
file system, terminal, log"}}:::svc TOOLS("shell tools
topic, node, param, logview") end KERNEL[["microkernel
threads, scheduling,
memory, IPC, topics"]]:::kern NODE -->|"topics"| KERNEL SVC -->|"requests"| KERNEL DRV --> KERNEL SRV --> KERNEL TOOLS --> KERNEL class USER zone ``` *Your nodes and services, the drivers, the servers and the tools are all separate user-space processes; the microkernel underneath provides only threads, scheduling, memory, IPC and topics.* The kernel does as little as it can: it creates processes and threads, schedules them by priority, isolates their memory, and carries messages between them. Everything else runs as an ordinary process with its own address space, so a fault in a driver or a server cannot corrupt the kernel or another program.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| | Periodic node | Aperiodic service |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | once per declared period: wake, read inputs, compute, publish | once per request: receive, handle, reply exactly once |
| Talks over | topics: many readers, the latest value | requests: one client, one reply |
| You write | one function with a `#[periodic]` attribute | a trait, its implementation, and a client call |
| Typical use | sensor drivers, estimators, controllers, actuator commands | device drivers, configuration, anything asked for on demand |

A **periodic node** is the shape most robot code takes. You declare its period, what it
does on an overrun, and what it reads and publishes; the framework owns the loop:

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn brake(
    #[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] range: Cycle<Range>,
    #[publish(CMD_VELOCITY)] command: Out<Twist>,
) {
    command.publish(match range.get() {
        Some(reading) if reading.range > 0.30 => cruise(),
        _ => stop(),   // too close, no reading, or a reading too old
    });
}
```

What the framework does for every node:

- **Fixed timing.** Each release wakes at an absolute time on the period's grid, so the
  period never drifts. An overrun is detected, handled by the declared policy, and
  reported.
- **Freshness.** Each input has a `stale_after` bound. A reading that never arrived and a
  reading that is too old are the same case, `None`, so a node cannot act on stale data
  by accident.
- **All-or-nothing outputs.** What the body publishes goes out when the body returns, in
  declaration order. A body that panics halfway publishes nothing.

An **aperiodic service** is a server: a client calls it and blocks until the one reply
arrives. Drivers are services, and so is anything an application asks for on demand.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
A topic is a named stream of fixed-size values, with any number of readers. Each reader
gets the latest value; a slow reader misses values but never blocks the writer. A topic is
defined once, in a crate both ends import, with its name, its payload type and its
**lane**:

```rust
pub const SENSOR_RANGE: Topic<Range, SafeLane>   = Topic::new("sensor/range");
pub const CMD_VELOCITY: Topic<Twist, KernelLane> = Topic::new("cmd/velocity");
```

| Lane | How a value travels | Safety class |
|---|---|---|
| `KernelLane` | copied in and out by the kernel, one system call per message; payloads up to 4 KiB | safety |
| `SafeLane` | zero-copy through shared memory; the kernel lets the writer change only the slot it is filling, so a published value cannot be corrupted | safety |
| `FastLane` | zero-copy through shared memory, no system call per message, no such protection | quality-managed |

Changing a topic's lane is a one-word edit to its definition; no node changes. A node
declared `safety` refuses to build if it reads or publishes a topic on a quality-managed
lane.

Both ends of a topic must agree on the payload. Every payload type has a **layout
identity** computed from its fields, and an end whose payload differs in size or layout
is refused when it opens the topic, with a message that says why.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
- **Standard payloads** (`robot_messages`): `Vector3`, `Point`, `Quaternion`, `Pose`,
  `Twist`, `Range`, `Imu`, `Odometry`, in SI units; sensor and odometry records carry a
  time stamp in nanoseconds since boot.
  Rust and Python read the same definitions, and the Python module is generated from the
  Rust structs by the build.
- **Your own payloads** are plain structs that derive `WirePlain`, which proves at build
  time that they have no padding and computes their layout identity.
- **Coordinate frames** (`frames`): a robot's frames are declared once as a tree, checked
  at build time, and looked up with `lookup(target, source)`, with no allocation and a
  bounded cost. A moving link takes its value from a node input, so it goes stale like any
  other input.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| Feature | What you get |
|---|---|
| Run-time parameters | declare a gain with a default and a range; change it from the shell with `param set` while the node runs |
| Actions | a long-running goal (drive to a point, home an axis) with feedback, cancel and a dead-man lease |
| Release journal | every node with an output journals each release, so a recording can replay it |
| Description | every node announces its period, inputs, outputs and parameters, which `node info` prints |

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
```text
tsh> topic record -o /recordings/run7.mcap &     record every topic
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &                     run the robot
tsh> brake --replay /recordings/run7.mcap        re-run one node against what it saw
replay: brake life 1: 2104 releases, 2103 compared, identical
```

Recordings are standard MCAP files. Replaying a node runs its body once per recorded
release, with exactly the inputs, parameters and timing that release had, and compares
every output. An edited node replays too, which answers "what would it have done?".

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
| | Rust | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Periodic nodes | `#[periodic]` attribute | `@periodic` decorator |
| Parameters, actions, record and replay | yes | yes |
| Coordinate frames | yes | not yet |
| Services and device classes | yes | no |

A Rust node and a Python node exchange topics with each other; both use the same
transports.

chunks.docTitle: Robot Applications on TAIL OS: Concepts
chunks.text:
- TailOS targets the Raspberry Pi 3. The robotics framework is tested on the QEMU
  emulation of that board. The Python interpreter is not yet on the board image.
- No process supervisor ships: a node that exits is not restarted.
- Run-time parameter values last for the node's life; a restart starts at the defaults.

chunks.text:
- [Periodic nodes in Rust](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md)
- [Periodic nodes in Python](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md)

Write a function, name its period and its topics, and TAIL OS runs it on time.

**Read this first**

- **What you need:** the Raspberry Pi 3 board support package (BSP) with the TAIL OS SDK, and a Rust function to run.
- **What you get:** a node that runs on a fixed period, reads and publishes topics, and needs no `main`, thread, sleep or retry loop.
- **Time to a first node:** one file of 24 lines, one line in `tail.build`, and one build of the disk image.

This page is the Rust API. The [Python page](periodic_python_public.md) describes the Python API.

**Contents**

- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Your first nodes](#your-first-nodes)
- [`#[periodic]` keys](#periodic-keys)
- [Node shapes](#node-shapes)
- [Several inputs](#several-inputs)
- [`Cycle<T>`](#cyclet)
- [Run-time parameters](#run-time-parameters)
- [Actions](#actions)
- [The release journal](#the-release-journal)
- [Recording and replay](#recording-and-replay)
- [Start-up](#start-up)
- [`OverrunPolicy`](#overrunpolicy)
- [Topics and lanes](#topics-and-lanes)
- [Raw ends](#raw-ends)
- [Durations](#durations)
- [Payloads](#payloads)
- [Frames and transforms](#frames-and-transforms)
- [`NodeError`](#nodeerror)
- [Migrating a node](#migrating-a-node)
- [`Executor`](#executor)
- [Glossary](#glossary)

A **node** is a function that TAIL OS runs once every period. Each run is a **release**.
You would otherwise write a thread with a timer loop: read the clock, do the work, sleep
for the rest of the period, correct the drift, repeat. The framework runs that loop for
you.

A node has **inputs**, the topics it reads, and **outputs**, the topics it publishes. You
declare each one on the parameter that receives it. Each input has its own freshness bound.

1. Save the file as `app/counter/src/main.rs` in the BSP.
2. Add `/usr/bin/counter=counter` to the `[disk]` section of the BSP's `tail.build`.
3. Run `./make-disk.sh`. It builds the program against the SDK and puts it in `/usr/bin` on the image ([Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](../../../doc/install_rpi3.md#add-your-own-programs)).

You write no `Cargo.toml` and no `main`: the attribute writes the `main`.

On the booted image, start the node in the background and look at it:

```text
tsh> counter &
tsh> node list
counter  pid 5  counter
tsh> topic echo -n 3 --as "count:u64 stamp_ns:u64" counter/releases
# counter/releases: kernel lane, --as, 16 B, layout 0x79e81151
count=1 stamp_ns=161062928
count=2 stamp_ns=260987952
count=3 stamp_ns=360967504
```

`node list` shows each running node: its name, its process and its program. Your pid and
counts differ. `topic echo` reads the topic as any other program would. `--as` names the
payload's fields, because `Releases` is not a standard payload that `topic echo` decodes on
its own. Each count is one more release. The
[shell tools](../../../utility/doc/shell_tools_public.md) page describes both tools.

Three nodes share two topics. A **topic** is a named channel that carries one payload type. The **lane** is how a topic's messages travel from publisher to readers. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: The three nodes of your first nodes and their topics accDescr: lidar runs every 20 ms and publishes sensor/range on the safe lane, which brake and drive both read. drive also reads cmd/velocity on the kernel lane, published by a pad or a planner that this page does not write. lidar("lidar
every 20 ms"):::prog range(["sensor/range
SafeLane"]):::chan brake("brake
every 20 ms"):::prog drive("drive
every 20 ms"):::prog velocity(["cmd/velocity
KernelLane"]):::chan pad("a pad, a planner
(not written here)"):::ext lidar --> range range --> brake range --> drive pad --> velocity velocity --> drive ``` *lidar publishes `sensor/range`, which brake and drive read; drive also reads `cmd/velocity` from a pad or planner not written here.* The example is four files in the BSP's `app/` directory: | File | Holds | |---|---| | `app/robot_topics.rs` | the topics: each one's name, payload and lane | | `app/lidar/src/main.rs` | a node that publishes `sensor/range` | | `app/brake/src/main.rs` | a node that reads `sensor/range` | | `app/drive/src/main.rs` | a node that reads `sensor/range` and `cmd/velocity` |

1. Add `/usr/bin/lidar=lidar`, `/usr/bin/brake=brake` and `/usr/bin/drive=drive` to the `[disk]` section of the BSP's `tail.build`.
2. Run `./make-disk.sh`. It builds each `app/<name>/src/main.rs` against the SDK's `periodic` crate and puts it in `/usr/bin` on the image. See [Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](../../../doc/install_rpi3.md#add-your-own-programs).
3. On the booted image, start the nodes in the background, in any order: `lidar &`, `brake &`, `drive &`.

A program's name is at most 32 bytes. A longer name is left out of the image's program
table, so the program never starts and leaves no record.

No program names another. The framework opens each topic and waits for its publisher
(see [Start-up](#start-up)). Nothing here publishes `cmd/velocity`, so `drive` runs and
stays stopped: that input is absent, and absent takes the `_` arm.

`periodic`, `wire_plain` and `robot_messages` are SDK libraries, so a program needs only
a `use` for each. Two lines exist only because the BSP's one-file programs share a file:

| Line | Why |
|---|---|
| `#[path = "../../robot_topics.rs"] mod robot_topics;` | compiles the shared definitions file into this program |
| `#![allow(dead_code)]`, in the definitions file | stops a warning in each program that leaves a definition unused |

**In a cargo workspace, the definitions are a library crate.** Then
`robot_topics/src/lib.rs` needs no `#![allow(dead_code)]`. Each program lists `periodic`
and `robot_topics` in its `Cargo.toml` and starts at its `use` lines. A payload that a
Python program also reads lives in its own crate that depends on `wire_plain` alone. The
host generator that prints its Python definitions imports that crate, and it cannot import
a crate that depends on `periodic`.

The rest of this page shows each program from its `use` lines on, with its topics
imported from `robot_topics`.

The build compiles the Quick start's `counter` and every file of Your first nodes, byte
for byte as shown, and runs `counter` on the emulated Raspberry Pi 3. The build also
checks every refusal under [What the build refuses](#what-the-build-refuses) against the
text shown. Some short examples further down are variations written for this page and are
not compiled.

The header states what is true of the whole node. Each input and each output is declared
on its own parameter.

| Where | Key | Required |
|---|---|---|
| header | `every = "<duration>"` | always |
| header | `on_overrun = Skip \| CatchUp \| Fault` | always |
| header | `init = <expr>` | exactly when the body takes a state |
| header | `safety` | no |
| parameter | `#[subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after = "<duration>")]` | once per input |
| parameter | `#[publish(TOPIC)]` | once per output |
| parameter | `#[param(default = .., range = .. ..= ..)]` | once per run-time parameter |
| parameter | `#[serve(ACTION, lease = "<duration>")]` | at most once per node |

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
```

The **period**: the time from one release to the next, written as a
[duration](#durations). Releases fall on `start + n * period`, so they never drift.

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
```

An **overrun** is a release whose body runs past the next release. `on_overrun` says
what happens then: `Skip`, `CatchUp` or `Fault`, written as the bare word. There is no
default, so a node without it does not compile. See [`OverrunPolicy`](#overrunpolicy).

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn brake(#[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] lidar: Cycle<Range>) {
    brake_for(lidar.get().map_or(0.0, |reading| reading.range));
}
```

The parameter is one input: the topic, then **`stale_after`**, how old a reading may be
before this node reads it as absent.

A **`Cycle<T>`** is one input's view of one release. The node gets one per input.

```rust
#[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] lidar: Cycle<Range>,
```

An input is in one of three states:

| State | `get()` | `was_stale()` | `since_received()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| nothing received since the node started | `None` | `false` | `None` |
| received, and no older than `stale_after` | `Some(&T)` | `false` | `Some(age)` |
| received, and older than `stale_after` | `None` | `true` | `Some(age)` |

`Cycle` is not `Send`, so moving one to another thread is a compile error. The node opens and reads its inputs on the one thread that runs it. Whether `SafeLane` and `FastLane` ends work from another thread is not established, so nothing of an input leaves its thread.

```rust
match lidar.get() {
    Some(reading) => brake_for(reading.range),
    None => brake_for(0.0), // absent or stale
}
```

Returns the reading if one was received and is no older than `stale_after`. A stale reading returns `None`, the same as no reading, so the fail-safe branch is the default branch. The comparison is strict: a reading exactly `stale_after` old is still usable.

```rust
let reading: Option<Range> = lidar.copied();
```

Returns the same reading as a copy you own. `get()` lends the framework's one held copy and makes no copy of its own.

```rust
if lidar.missed() > 0 {
    count_dropped(lidar.missed());
}
```

Returns the publications the lane lost for this input, seen by this release's reads. It is **not** a running total.

Each lane counts its own losses, and they mean different things. Take a 200 ms node that reads a 50 ms publisher:

| Lane | `missed()` counts | What the 200 ms node sees |
|---|---|---|
| `SafeLane`, `FastLane` | publications that newer ones overtook before this reader got them | the newest of four, and `missed()` = 3 on every release; nothing is wrong |
| `KernelLane` | publications the topic overwrote before the node read them | the newest of four, and `missed()` = 0: the other three were still in the topic, passed over, not lost. The topic keeps at least its newest 8. |

Limits:

- **`missed() == 0` does not mean the node saw every publication.** On `KernelLane` a publication passed over for a newer one is not counted.
- **A non-zero `missed()` is not always a fault.** On `SafeLane`, a publisher faster than its reader is counted on every release.
- **A `KernelLane` input counts loss from the moment it opened.** It neither hands over nor counts what was published before.

```rust
if lidar.rejected() > 0 {
    count_rejected(lidar.rejected());
}
```

Returns the publications the lane refused on this input since the last release. It is not a running total.

| Lane | When it rejects |
|---|---|
| `SafeLane` | a malformed publication, at read; the next release reads again |
| `FastLane` | a frame that fails validation, counted again on every release until its writer replaces it |
| `KernelLane` | never: `rejected()` is always 0, because a writer of another payload is refused when it opens (see [Payloads](#payloads)) |

```rust
#[subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after = "70ms")] range: Cycle<Range>,
```

The framework measures age from **receipt at this node**, on the clock the node's releases run on. A reading the body acts on:

- arrived no more than `stale_after` ago;
- was published no earlier than `stale_after` plus the gap since the previous read. That gap is one period in steady state.

Limits:

- **After a late wake-up, the gap is the whole delay, and that release is not told.** The drive node runs every 20 ms with a 310 ms command bound. It is kept off the processor for one second. Meanwhile its planner publishes one last command and dies. The first release after the stall gets that command as new: `since_received()` is zero, `arrived()` is true, `overruns()` is zero. The node drives on it for 310 ms more. `overruns()` reports the missed releases on the release after.
- **A bound shorter than the node's period is accepted.** With `every = "20ms"`, `stale_after = "5ms"` and a 40 ms publisher, the input is usable on the release a publication arrives and stale on the next, for ever.
- **Nothing checks the sizing rule below.**

```
stale_after >= (lost publications tolerated + 1) x the publisher's period + this node's period
```

Then move it half a node period off: never write a multiple of the node's period.

| Input | Publisher | Tolerates | Rule | Written |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `range` of the 20 ms drive node | every 20 ms | 1 lost | `2 x 20 + 20 = 60` | `"70ms"` |
| `permit` of the 20 ms drive node | every 50 ms | 1 lost | `2 x 50 + 20 = 120` | `"130ms"` |

Why half a period off: the age a node sees is a whole number of its own periods, give or take wake-up jitter. With `"60ms"` on a 20 ms node, a reading is 60 ms old three releases later, a few microseconds either way. Whether it is still usable then depends on which wake-up ran later. `"70ms"` decides it 10 ms away from any release.

A node judges only at a release. So it drops an input between `stale_after` and `stale_after` plus two periods after the publisher's last publication, plus any scheduling delay.

```rust
#[periodic(every = "5ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
fn balance(
    #[subscribe(IMU, stale_after = "12ms")] imu: Cycle<Imu>,
    #[param(default = 42.0, range = 0.0..=200.0)] kp: f32,
    #[param(default = 1.5, range = 0.0..=20.0)] kd: f32,
    #[publish(MOTOR_COMMAND)] command: Out<MotorCommand>,
) {
    command.publish(match imu.get() {
        Some(imu) => MotorCommand::torque(kp * imu.pitch + kd * imu.pitch_rate),
        None => MotorCommand::STOP,
    });
}
```

A **parameter** is a value you tune while the node runs: a gain, a limit, a flag. You
declare it on the argument that receives it, with its default and its range. The body is
handed each value by value on every release, and reading one costs nothing.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Name | The argument's name, at most 23 bytes. |
| Type | One of `bool`, `i32`, `i64`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, written as the type itself. |
| `range` | Names both ends and includes them. Required for every type but `bool`, which takes none: `#[param(default = false)] armed: bool`. |
| Default and bounds | May be named constants. The build checks them. |
| Count | At most 16 parameters per node. |

shell tool"):::prog request(["balance/__param_set
KernelLane"]):::chan balance("balance
every 5 ms"):::prog state(["balance/__params
KernelLane"]):::chan param --> request request --> balance balance --> state state -.-> param ``` *`param` writes a request; the node applies it and answers with its state.* ```text tsh> param list balance kp = 42.0 (0.0 .. 200.0) kd = 1.5 (0.0 .. 20.0) tsh> param set balance kp 45.5 balance: kp = 45.5 from release 18342 tsh> param list balance kp = 45.5 (0.0 .. 200.0, default 42.0) kd = 1.5 (0.0 .. 20.0) tsh> param set balance kp 250 param: balance kp = 250.0 is outside 0.0 .. 200.0; nothing was set tsh> param list balance 2 parameters ``` - **A set takes effect at the start of a release.** The release that `param set` names is the first one whose body gets the new value. A body never sees a value change while it runs. - **`param set` reports success only when the node answers.** It exits 1 when the node refuses, or does not answer within eight of its periods plus 250 ms. - **Set coupled gains in one command.** `param set balance kp 50 kd 2.5` is one request, applied whole at one release. Two commands are two requests: at least one release runs with the new `kp` and the old `kd`. - **The node checks every request** against the declared range, both ends included. It refuses a value outside the range, a NaN, or an unknown name, and nothing changes. `param` refuses the same values before it sends. - **Values last for the node's life.** A restart or a reboot starts at the defaults again. To keep a value, change its default in the source. `param list` shows each changed value beside its default, so you can copy it. - **A node declared `safety` has no parameters.** Its configuration is part of its verified build. `#[param]` on it fails the build; make the value a `const`. - **`param` logs each applied change** in its own ring of the system log: `balance: kp 42.0 -> 45.5 from release 18342` (`logview -s param`). A program that writes the request topic itself leaves no log record; the change is still in the node's state and its release journal. - **Replay hands each body the values it ran with.** A recording across sets replays as `identical`. Renaming, retyping, adding, removing or reordering a parameter makes a new declaration, which replay refuses. A changed default or range still replays. - **`node list` shows every node; `param list` shows only nodes with parameters.** `node info balance` prints `Parameters: 2, settable` when they can be set.

- **One non-blocking read per release**, of the request topic, before the body. Almost
  always it finds nothing. A release that finds a request also checks up to 16 values and
  publishes the node's state. All of it counts inside the cycle that overrun accounting
  measures.
- **Two kernel-lane topics per node**, `<node>/__params` and `<node>/__param_set`. Count
  them in the image's `[topic]` budget: two table entries, plus 2 pages for up to two
  parameters, or 8 pages for 16.
- **Without those topics the node runs on its defaults** and cannot be set. This happens
  when topic storage is full, or a recorder still holds the topics of an earlier run with
  another parameter table. The node says so once, at WARNING, before its first release:

```text
balance: no parameter topics (topic storage full); runs with its defaults
```

- **Load a settable node whose timing matters from the boot image, not from the FAT
  disk.** A node loaded from FAT pages its request-handling code in from the disk during
  the release that handles its first request.
- **Any program can set a parameter**, within its range, by writing the request topic.
  No topic has writer authorisation yet. A value outside the range never reaches a body.

The **lease** is how long a goal survives without a keep-alive from its client. The handle
sends a keep-alive once per server period while it is polled. When the keep-alives stop,
the node stops the goal at the end of the lease, and the goal ends `Abandoned`. That covers
a client that was killed, crashed, hung, or simply stopped polling.

- **The lease is required and must be at least twice the period.** `lease = "39ms"` on a
  20 ms node does not start: `could not start: lease 39ms is shorter than twice the period
  20ms`.
- **Choose about five periods**, for example `lease = "100ms"` on a 20 ms node. That rides
  out a lost keep-alive, a client one period late, and a client node up to four periods
  slow.
- **A killed client's goal stops within the lease plus two periods.** At 20 ms and 100 ms
  that is about 140 ms after the last keep-alive, plus release lateness. No death signal
  stops it sooner.
- **A periodic client slower than the lease loses every goal.** It polls once per its own
  release. A client every 150 ms against a 100 ms lease sees each goal end `Abandoned`.
  Make the lease longer than the slowest client's period plus one server period.
- **A program that stops polling loses its goal.** In
  `let drive = DRIVE_TO.send(goal)?; long_work(); drive.wait()`, the goal is abandoned
  during `long_work`. Call `poll`, `feedback` or `wait` while the goal should run.

chunks.text:
- **One non-blocking read per release** of the request topic, which almost always finds
  nothing. **One status publish per release**, of at most 4096 bytes. Both count inside the
  cycle that overrun accounting measures. Nothing is allocated and nothing is logged.
- **Two kernel-lane topics per action**, `<action>/__goal` and `<action>/__status`. Count
  them in the image's `[topic]` budget: two table entries, plus the pages for a goal record
  (24 bytes plus the goal) and a status (176 bytes plus the feedback and the result).
- **A serving node whose action topics cannot be opened does not start.** It names the
  action: `drive: could not start: action drive_to: drive_to/__goal: topic storage full`.
- **Replay hands each body the goal it ran with** and opens no action topic. Replay does
  not compare feedback or results, only the node's outputs.
- **Any program can send, keep, cancel or replace a goal** by writing the request topic
  with another process's id. No topic has writer authorisation yet. The lease, and the
  device's own lease, remain the stop.

```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: One release of the lidar node and its journal record accDescr: The lidar node reads the clock, samples its inputs, publishes record k on lidar/__releases on the kernel lane, then runs its body and publishes its outputs. sample("release k
sleep, read the clock,
sample the inputs") journal(["lidar/__releases
KernelLane"]):::chan body("run the body") outputs("publish each output
in declaration order") sample --> journal journal --> body body --> outputs ``` *The record of release k goes out before the body runs.* The **release journal** is one record per release that every node with an output publishes on a kernel-lane topic of its own, `/__releases`. `` is the node function's name: `lidar` publishes `lidar/__releases`. You write nothing for it, and you cannot turn it off. A node with no output has no journal. The journal is what a recording needs to replay a node exactly. The record goes out **before** the body runs, so a body that panics or hangs still leaves its release behind. | Record k carries | Detail | |---|---| | The release | `k`, the clock reading, the overruns delivered, and the publishing process. | | Each input | Arrived, missed, rejected, and the reading if it arrived (zeros if not). | | Each parameter | The value release k's body is handed. | | Release k-1's outputs | What became of each (none, declined, published, refused), and each payload end to end in declaration order (zeros for one not published). | - **Size:** 32 bytes plus the inputs' facts and payloads, 8 bytes per parameter and the outputs' payloads, all rounded up to 8. At most 4096 bytes, the kernel lane's limit. - **Layout identity:** the node's declaration: its period, overrun policy, each input's payload type, each parameter's name and type, and each output's payload type, in order. `topic list` shows it as `layout 0x…`. - **No journal:** a node with more than 16 outputs, or whose record would pass 4096 bytes, runs without one and logs a WARNING that says why.

- **One kernel-lane publish per release**, of at most 4096 bytes, before the body. It never
  waits for a reader. It counts inside the cycle that overrun accounting measures, so a
  journal that makes a release late shows up as an overrun.
- **One topic in the image's `[topic]` budget** per node with an output: one table entry
  and the record's pages. Count it when you size `[topic]` in `tail.build`.

  | Record size | Pages |
  |---|---|
  | up to 192 bytes | 1 |
  | up to 384 bytes | 2 |
  | 1 KiB | 5 |
  | 4 KiB | 20 |

- **4 KiB of stack** in every node with an output, journal or not. It is the buffer each

When the journal cannot be opened, the node runs exactly as it would with one. This
happens when topic storage is full, the record would pass 4096 bytes, or the topic is held
with another declaration's layout. The node says so once, at WARNING, before its first
release:

```text
brake: no release journal (topic storage full); this run cannot be replayed
```

Every node, with an output or not, also publishes its description on `<node>/__node`.
`node list` and `node info` read it ([shell tools](../../../utility/doc/shell_tools_public.md#node)).
It takes one kernel-lane topic, and one page for a node of a few inputs and outputs (a
record up to 192 bytes). Count it in `[topic]` too. When it cannot be opened, the node runs
unlisted and says so once, at WARNING, before its first release:

```text
brake: no node description (topic storage full); node list does not show this node
```

**A node's name must be unique within an image.** Two node functions with the same name
share one journal topic. If their declarations differ, the second finds the topic held with
another layout and runs without a journal. The same program started twice also shares one
journal: its records interleave, each names its process, and replay refuses them.

A Python node journals through the same record:
[its page](periodic_python_public.md#recording-and-replay) says how.

```text
tsh> topic record -o /recordings/run7.mcap &        FIRST: before the nodes
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &
     ... the run ...
tsh> brake --replay /recordings/run7.mcap
replay: brake life 1: 2104 releases, 2103 compared, identical
facts: sensor/range: 5 releases without an arrival, 3 missed, 0 rejected; cmd/velocity: 0, 0, 0; 1 overruns
replay: running release 2103, the life's last; its output is in no record
```

You record a run, then run one node of it again, offline, against exactly what it saw.
Nothing in the node changes: replay reads the node's [release journal](#the-release-journal),
and the generated `main` reads the options.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--replay FILE` | Replay the node from the recording. Goes **at the end** of the node's own command line. |
| `--life N` | After `--replay FILE`: pick a later life of the node. A restart during the recording is life 2. |

Replay runs the node's `init`, then its body once per recorded release. It hands each
input the reading, loss counts and overruns that release had, and each parameter its value,
at the recorded clock reading. It opens no topic, publishes nothing and never sleeps. It
compares what the body hands each output with what the node published, release by release.
A difference names the output by its topic, and the command exits 1:

```text
replay: brake life 1: first divergence at release 2059:
  output cmd/brake byte 0: recorded 00 00 00 00, replayed 9a 99 19 3e
replay: 1 of 2103 compared releases differ
```

Replay recomputes each input's age and staleness, and the body, with the binary you run.
So an edited body or a changed `stale_after` is a what-if: "would brake have stopped
earlier with `stale_after = "40ms"`?"

Replay refuses a changed declaration and names both versions:

| Changed | Replays |
|---|---|
| The body | yes |
| `stale_after` | yes |
| A parameter's default or range | yes |
| An input's or output's type or order | no |
| The period or the overrun policy | no |
| A parameter's name, type or order | no |

- **Start `topic record` before the nodes.** Otherwise the journal is not whole from the
  first release, and replay refuses:
  `life 1 starts at release 37: the recorder attached after brake started; start topic record before the nodes`.
  A node faster than every 15 ms can lose its first records even so.
- **The last release runs uncompared.** Its output is in no record, because the node was
  stopped, crashed, or the recording ended. Replay prints its verdict first, then runs it.
  A body that crashed in the recording crashes the same way in the replay.
- **Replay runs `init` and the body as written.** A node that opens a device does so in a
  replay too. Replay such a node only where the device is absent, or replay the nodes
  downstream of it instead.
- **What replay cannot see shows up as a divergence**, never as a false `identical`: time
  read other than through `periodic::now()` or a `Cycle`, side effects other than the
  outputs, the node's own command-line arguments (give the same ones), anything that
  depends on `HashMap` order.
- **A node with no output cannot be replayed.** There is nothing to compare, and replay
  refuses before `init` runs.
- **A journal the recorder lost part of** replays up to the lost stretch, and claims
  nothing for the rest.
- **Output streams:** the verdict is on standard output. Refusals are on standard error and
  exit 1. A malformed `--replay ...` tail exits 2.

in the order written") inputs("open each input, in the order written

KernelLane: opens at once") action("serving node: open the action topics
goal reader, then status writer;
a refusal fails the start") journal("node with an output: open the journal
a refusal is one WARNING") description("every node: open its description
a refusal is one WARNING") check --> outputs outputs --> inputs inputs --> action action --> journal journal --> description ``` *Outputs open before inputs; the journal and the description open last.* ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: How a node starts running accDescr: Once every topic is open, the node drops what each input holds, starts its release grid at release 0, then runs every release: sleep, read the clock, sample the inputs, publish the journal record, run the body, publish each output. drop("drop what each input holds
one read each") zero("release 0

You write no retry loop and no start-up order. - **Outputs open first, in the order written.** Two nodes that read each other then both start: each creates its topics before it waits for the other's. - **A served action opens after the inputs**, its goal reader before its status writer. A client sends only after it reads a status, so it never sends to a reader that does not exist yet. A refusal fails the start and names the action (see [Actions](#actions)). - **The journal and the description open last**, so they never take a table entry that one of the node's own topics needs. A refusal of either does not stop the node (see [The release journal](#the-release-journal)). - **One wait budget for the whole node:** 2 000 "nobody publishes this yet" answers, 5 ms apart, about ten seconds whatever the number of inputs. On a busy system each wait can run longer, so the start can take longer to fail. Only that answer is waited on; any other refusal ends the start at once. - **Nothing published before the start reaches the node.** Each input's collected readings are dropped, and loss from before the start is not reported.

- **A node does not run until every topic it declares is open.** The drive node with no
  `lidar` waits ten seconds, writes one ERROR record and exits with status 1; its body
  never runs. The rest of the system sees only silence on the topics it would publish.
- **A kernel-lane input never fails the start for absence.** Subscribing creates the
  topic. So a kernel-lane topic nobody publishes, or a misspelt name, starts fine and that
  input stays absent for ever. The topic goes away when the node ends.
- **An early kernel-lane input waits too.** Inputs open in the order written, so it may
  wait ten seconds for a later input's publisher. What is published meanwhile is dropped
  at the start.
- **Only the first missing topic is named.** With three safe-lane publishers down, it takes
  three ten-second runs to learn all three.
- **An output created before a failed start stays without a writer.** A downstream node is
  admitted against it and receives nothing. The failed node writes one record per output it
  created (see [`NodeError`](#nodeerror)). On `KernelLane` the topic goes away with its last
  end, so a restarted node can create it again.
- **Release 0 can show a reading published during start-up.** A publication that lands
  between an input's drop and release 0's sampling is handed over at release 0. What holds
  is that nothing published before the start is shown.
- **A topic published once, or only on change, cannot be an input.** A node that starts
  after the publication never receives it.
- **A mistyped duration fails the start, not the build.** See [Durations](#durations).

| Your node | Use | Keeps |
|---|---|---|
| Its deadline **is** the safety requirement | `Fault` | nothing: the node stops |
| Integrates or counts, and must see every interval exactly once | `CatchUp` | the count of releases |
| Anything else, such as a control loop | `Skip` | the phase of the grid |

```rust
#[periodic(every = "20ms", on_overrun = Skip)]
```

The node abandons the missed releases and resumes on the grid. Use it for a control loop,
where a late command computed from stale inputs is worse than none.

The brake and drive nodes both read it. lidar("lidar"):::prog --> range(["sensor/range
SafeLane"]):::chan --> brake("brake"):::prog range --> drive("drive"):::prog ``` *lidar publishes `sensor/range` on `SafeLane`; brake and drive read it.*

```rust
pub const CMD_VELOCITY: Topic<Twist, KernelLane> = Topic::new("cmd/velocity");

```

A **lane** is the way a topic's payloads travel from the publisher to the readers. TAIL OS has three.

| Lane | Publishers | Copies | May carry safety data |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KernelLane` | up to 4 at once | 1 in, 1 out to each reader | yes |
| `SafeLane` | exactly 1 | none | yes |
| `FastLane` | exactly 1 | none | **no** |

A reader is handed the latest value on every lane. A `KernelLane` topic also keeps its newest 8 publications, which a tool such as `topic echo` can show.

`KernelLane` carries payloads of at most 4 KiB. A larger payload on it does not compile: `a kernel-lane payload is at most 4096 bytes`. `SafeLane` and `FastLane` copy nothing, because the publisher and the readers share memory.

Take the first row that matches your topic.

| Your topic | Use |
|---|---|
| Has more than one publisher | `KernelLane` |
| Carries a small payload | `KernelLane` |
| Carries a large payload, and a reader has a safety requirement | `SafeLane` |
| Carries a large payload, and nothing that reads it has a safety requirement | `FastLane` |

A copy-free lane is not always faster. For a small payload, the copy costs less than setting up shared memory. The crossover is about 2 KB, an estimate that has not been measured.

Two nodes that import one definition cannot disagree. Two programs that each write their own definition of one name can. The result depends on what differs.

| What differs | Result |
|---|---|
| The payload, in size or in layout | The node that opens second does not start. Its record says what the topic carries (see [Payloads](#payloads)). |
| The lane: the publisher on `SafeLane` or `FastLane`, the reader on `KernelLane` | The reader starts and receives nothing, with no error. |
| The lane: the publisher on `KernelLane`, the reader on `SafeLane` or `FastLane` | The reader's node does not start: ``could not start: topic `cmd/velocity` never appeared``. |
| The lane: `SafeLane` against `FastLane` | The reader's node does not start, and its record does not name the lane: on a `SafeLane` reader it says `this is not the payload type the topic carries`, on a `FastLane` reader `the topic could not be joined`. |

No record names the lane as the cause. Known issue: TAIL-489. Two payload types with one layout under two names, such as `Point` and `Vector3`, are one payload to every lane.

Each convention is written in the doc comment of a `robot_messages` payload. The build copies it into `tail_messages`, so a Python node reads the same words. These are the conventions most robotics software already uses.

| Convention | Stated on |
|---|---|
| Right-handed; a body frame has x forward, y left, z up; SI units: m, rad, s | `Vector3`, `Point`, `Pose` |
| Positive angles turn counter-clockwise about the axis (right-hand rule): a yaw of +15 degrees turns left | `Quaternion` |
| Hamilton algebra (i*j = k); stored x, y, z, w, with w the scalar; q and -q are one rotation; the identity is (0, 0, 0, 1); all four zero means "not estimated" and is not a rotation | `Quaternion` |
| Roll, pitch and yaw are about fixed axes: R = Rz(yaw)*Ry(pitch)*Rx(roll) | `Quaternion` |
| A pose used as a transform is the pose of the child frame in the parent frame, T_P_C, which takes p_C to p_P = R(q)*p_C + t; T_A_C = T_A_B * T_B_C | `Pose` |
| A transform rotates and translates a `Point`; it only rotates a `Vector3` (a direction, a velocity) | `Vector3`, `Point` |
| A range reading lies on the sensor frame's +x axis | `Range` |
| The standard frames: `map`, `odom`, `base_link`; `pose` is `base_link` in `odom`, `twist` is in the body frame | `Odometry` |

```rust
// app/robot_frames.rs

use frames::{frames, Angle};

frames! {
    /// The rover's coordinate frames, with the standard frame names.
    pub ROVER {
        /// World-fixed and continuous; drifts without bound.
        ODOM,
        /// The body: origin on the wheel axis, x forward, y left, z up.
        BASE_LINK moves in ODOM,
        /// The front range sensor: 0.10 m ahead of the wheel axis, turned 15 degrees left.
        RANGE_FRONT in BASE_LINK at { x: 0.10, yaw: Angle::from_degrees(15.0) },
    }
}
```

| Item | Is |
|---|---|
| `NodeFailure::reason()` | the `NodeError` |
| `NodeFailure::orphaned_publications()` | the outputs left without a writer, in declaration order; empty if none |
| `NodeFailure::records()` | `FailureRecord::Ended(reason)`, then one `FailureRecord::Orphaned(topic)` per orphaned output: one log record each |
| `Display` of `NodeFailure` | those records joined by `"; "`, for a place with room for one line |

A record of the system log holds 96 bytes after the `periodic` tag. That is why a failure
is several records, one fact each, and each record leads with its names.

- **A refused-open record can lose its end.** Its tail is the transport's reason, which can
  be long. The node and topic names always fit. The `NodeError` carries the whole reason.
- **A mistyped-duration record fits** while the node's name, the topic and the text are 36
  bytes or fewer together. Past that it loses its end, never the key or the start of the topic.
- **"Left without a writer" does not check other writers.** A `KernelLane` topic can have
  other writers, and one of them may still be alive.
- **A publisher your program opened itself is not named** (see [Raw ends](#raw-ends)).

| Record | Level | When |
|---|---|---|
| `<node>: missed 2 release(s)` | WARNING | after each cycle that was handed an overrun count |
| `<node>: 16 consecutive publishes to <topic> refused (<reason>); still trying` | ERROR | on the 16th refused publish in a row on one output |

The node keeps running after both records.

- **`missed N release(s)`**: act if it repeats. The node's work does not fit its period.
- **`16 consecutive publishes ... refused`**: act. Readers of that topic get nothing new. The
  record comes once per run of refusals. A new run starts after a publish on that output
  succeeds or the body declines to publish. Each output keeps its own count, and a refusal
  on one output does not stop the others.

`<reason>` is the transport's. On `SafeLane`, a publication the kernel refused is
`Refused`.

The body runs once on every release, whatever the transports answer.

A Python node writes the refused-publishes record, in the same words, to the console and
not to its log ring, so `logview` does not show it.

A declared period in ticks, or `None` if it is zero or cannot be represented.

**action**: a request that takes many releases, such as "drive to (2.0, 0.5)": a client
sends a goal, and the serving node reports feedback on every release and ends it with a
result.

**frame (coordinate frame)**: one of the robot's coordinate systems, declared once at build
time with `frames!`, so a lookup gives the transform between any two.

**goal**: one request of an action, sent by a client and lent to the serving node's body on
every release until it ends.

**input**: a topic a node reads, declared on a `Cycle<T>` parameter with
`#[subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after = "..")]`.

**lane**: how a topic's messages travel, written in the topic's type: `KernelLane` copies
through the kernel (up to 4 writers, 4 KiB), `SafeLane` shares memory with one writer and
may carry safety data, `FastLane` shares memory with one writer and may not.

**layout identity**: a 32-bit hash of a payload's fields, their order and types, which
`WirePlain` derives; an end whose identity differs from the topic's is refused at open.

**lease**: how long a served goal lives without its client's keep-alive, at least twice the
period, after which the node ends the goal `Abandoned`.

**node**: a function with `#[periodic(..)]` whose body the framework runs once on every
release.

**output**: a topic a node publishes, declared on an `Out<T>` parameter with
`#[publish(TOPIC)]` and published when the body returns.

**overrun**: a cycle that runs past its next release; `on_overrun` says what happens then.

**parameter**: a run-time parameter, a value declared with `#[param(default = .., range = ..)]`
that the shell can change while the node runs.

**payload**: the type a topic carries, a standard `robot_messages` record or your own
`#[repr(C)]` struct that derives `WirePlain`.

**period**: the interval `every` sets; releases fall on `start + n * period`.

**release**: one scheduled instant on the period's grid, at which the body runs once.

**release journal**: the record that every node with an output publishes on
`<node>/__releases` at every release, which replay reads.

**replay**: running one node again, offline, against a recording with `--replay FILE`, and
comparing its outputs with the recorded ones.

**stale_after**: an input's bound on how old a reading may be, measured from receipt at this
node, before it reads as absent.

**topic**: a named channel that carries one payload type on one lane, defined once as a
`Topic<Payload, Lane>` constant.

A **node** is a function that TAIL OS runs once every period. Each run is a **release**.
The framework runs the timing loop for you: it reads the clock, calls the function, and
sleeps for the rest of the period.

A node has **inputs**, the topics it reads, and **outputs**, the topics it publishes. You
declare each one on the parameter that receives it. Each input has its own freshness
bound. A node can also take run-time parameters that you tune from the shell, and serve
one [action](#actions): a goal a client sends it, which takes many releases.

`counter` is one file and one node. It runs every 100 ms, counts its releases, and
publishes the count:

```python
# counter.py

from periodic import periodic, publish, run, now, Payload, Skip, Topic

# What the counter publishes on every release: releases run so far, and when this one ran.
Releases = Payload("count:u64 stamp_ns:u64", "Releases")

# The counter's releases, published by the counter alone.
COUNTER_RELEASES = Topic("counter/releases", Releases, lane="kernel")

count = 0


@periodic(every="100ms", on_overrun=Skip)
def counter(releases=publish(COUNTER_RELEASES)):
    global count
    count += 1
    releases.publish(Releases.instance(count=count, stamp_ns=now()))


run()
```

- `@periodic` turns the function into a node, and `run()` runs it. The file has no loop and no sleep.
- `releases=publish(COUNTER_RELEASES)` is the node's output. The value the body hands to `releases.publish(..)` is published on `counter/releases` when the body returns.
- `count` lives at module level. That is how a Python node keeps state between releases.
- `Releases` is a **payload**, the type a topic carries. `Payload` lays it out exactly as the same struct in Rust.

Python and the `periodic` module are on the disk image of the
[QEMU download](../../../doc/install_qemu.md). On the booted image, write the file with
`vi /counter.py`, then start it in the background and look at it:

```text

tsh> topic echo -n 3 --as "count:u64 stamp_ns:u64" counter/releases
```

A topic is defined once, with three facts: its name, its payload and its lane. All three
belong to the topic, not to a node, because every end of a topic must agree on them. The
lane is `"kernel"`, `"safe"` or `"fast"`, and it has no default. A payload carries no

`examples/publisher.py`:

```python
from periodic import periodic, publish, run, monotonic_ns, Skip, Topic
from tail_messages import Range, RANGE_INFRARED

# The front ranger's readings, in the `range_front` frame.
FROM_PYTHON = Topic("pair/from_python", Range, lane="kernel")

count = 0


@periodic(every="20ms", on_overrun=Skip)
def sensor(reading=publish(FROM_PYTHON)):
    global count
    count += 1
    reading.publish(Range.instance(stamp_ns=monotonic_ns(), radiation_type=RANGE_INFRARED,
                                   field_of_view=0.05, min_range=0.02, max_range=4.0,
                                   range=0.25 * count, variance=0.0))


run()
```

An output is declared on the parameter that publishes it: `reading=publish(FROM_PYTHON)`.
On every release the body gets an `Out` in that parameter. `reading.publish(value)` hands
it the release's value, and the framework publishes it once the body returns. A body
returns nothing.

`RANGE_INFRARED` is one of `Range`'s named values, generated beside it. `count` keeps
state at module level; [below](#init-has-no-equivalent-and-does-not-need-one) is why
Python needs no `init` for that.

Pick the stamp clock by what the node does:

| The node | Stamps with |
|---|---|
| reads hardware, like `sensor` | `monotonic_ns()`: nanoseconds since boot, read when called, the instant it read the device |
| decides from its inputs | `now()`: the current release's one clock reading in nanoseconds, the instant every input was judged against; 0 before `run()` has opened the node |
| passes an input on | the input's own `stamp_ns` |

Both read the clock every `stamp_ns` field is in, the same one as `periodic::monotonic_ns()`
and `periodic::now()` in Rust. A replay of the node hands the body the recorded `now()`, so
a stamp from `now()` replays exactly; `monotonic_ns()` reads anew. See
[Recording and replay](#recording-and-replay).

A process is one node, so `now()` takes no argument. Call it from the body: from a thread
you started, it raises `RuntimeError`.

`examples/drive.py`, the whole program. It passes the commanded velocity on while the
range reading says the way is clear, and publishes a stop otherwise:

```python
from periodic import periodic, publish, run, subscribe, Skip, Topic
from tail_messages import Range, Twist, Vector3

# Velocity commands, in the `base_link` frame.
CMD_VELOCITY = Topic("cmd/velocity", Twist, lane="kernel")
# The front ranger's readings, in the `range_front` frame.
SENSOR_RANGE = Topic("sensor/range", Range, lane="safe")
# The velocity the drive is given, in the `base_link` frame.
DRIVE_VELOCITY = Topic("drive/velocity", Twist, lane="safe")

STOP_WITHIN_M = 0.3
STILL = Vector3.instance(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0)
STOP = Twist.instance(linear=STILL, angular=STILL)


@periodic(every="20ms", on_overrun=Skip)
def drive(command=subscribe(CMD_VELOCITY, stale_after="310ms"),
          lidar=subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after="70ms"),
          velocity=publish(DRIVE_VELOCITY)):
    twist, reading = command.get(), lidar.get()
    if twist is not None and reading is not None and reading.range > STOP_WITHIN_M:
        velocity.publish(twist)
    else:
        # The command or the range is absent or stale, or an obstacle is close.
        velocity.publish(STOP)


run()
```

Two inputs on two lanes, each with its own bound, and one output. The body gets one
`Cycle` per input and one `Out` per output, in the order the parameters are written. A
command may be 310 ms old and still be used; a range reading only 70 ms.

`get()` returns `None` both when nothing has arrived and when what it holds is older than
`stale_after`. So one `else` branch covers a sensor that goes quiet and a sensor that never
came up.

`Twist` nests two `Vector3`s, read as `twist.linear.x`, the name Rust uses. You build a
nested payload from instances of the payloads it nests.

Start the nodes in any order. A safe-lane input waits up to ten seconds for its
publisher; a kernel-lane input opens at once.

`examples/steer.py`, the whole program. It steers towards x = 2 m. It commands a velocity
on every release that has a usable odometry reading. On the releases the robot stands
still, it also reports where it stopped:

```python
from periodic import periodic, publish, run, subscribe, Payload, Skip, Topic
from tail_messages import Odometry, Twist, Vector3

DriveState = Payload("stamp_ns:u64 x:f64 y:f64", "DriveState")

# The robot's estimated pose and velocity, in the `odom` frame.
ODOMETRY = Topic("odometry", Odometry, lane="safe")
# Velocity commands, in the `base_link` frame.
CMD_VELOCITY = Topic("cmd/velocity", Twist, lane="kernel")
# Where the robot last stood still, in the `odom` frame.
DRIVE_STATE = Topic("drive/state", DriveState, lane="kernel")

GOAL_X_M = 2.0
GAIN_PER_S = 0.5
STILL_BELOW_M_S = 0.01

# Built once and rewritten on every release: an output keeps a reference until the body
# returns, and packs it then.
velocity = Twist.instance(linear=Vector3.instance(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0),
                          angular=Vector3.instance(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0))
stop = DriveState.instance(stamp_ns=0, x=0.0, y=0.0)


@periodic(every="20ms", on_overrun=Skip)
def drive(odometry=subscribe(ODOMETRY, stale_after="50ms"),
          command=publish(CMD_VELOCITY),
          state=publish(DRIVE_STATE)):
    reading = odometry.get()
    if reading is None:
        return                          # absent or stale: neither output publishes
    velocity.linear.x = GAIN_PER_S * (GOAL_X_M - reading.pose.position.x)
    command.publish(velocity)
    if abs(reading.twist.linear.x) < STILL_BELOW_M_S:
        stop.stamp_ns = reading.stamp_ns
        stop.x, stop.y = reading.pose.position.x, reading.pose.position.y
        state.publish(stop)


run()
```

Each output is its own parameter with its own `Out`. When the body returns, the framework
publishes every output that was handed a value, **in the order the outputs are declared**:
`command`, then `state`. The order the body handed them over in does not matter.

An output handed nothing publishes nothing at that release. Its readers keep what it last
published: here `drive/state` holds the last stop. A release with no usable reading
publishes neither output.

`publish` keeps a reference, not a copy, and packs the value when the body returns. So
`velocity` and `stop` can be built once and rewritten on every release. A change made after
`publish` but before the body returns is published. An output carries one publication per
release: a second `publish` at the same release raises `ValueError`. `DriveState` is the
example's own payload, declared with `Payload` ([Payloads](#payloads)).

parameter and served action is declared on its own parameter, as the parameter's default.

| Where | Written | Required |
|---|---|---|
| decorator | `every="<duration>"` | always |
| decorator | `on_overrun=Skip`, `CatchUp` or `Fault` | always |
| parameter | `name=subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after="<duration>")` | once per input |
| parameter | `name=publish(TOPIC)` | once per output |
| parameter | `name=param(default, range=(minimum, maximum))` | once per run-time parameter |
| parameter | `name=serve(ACTION, lease="<duration>")` | at most once per node |

A node reads, publishes or serves an action. One that does none of them is refused:

```
NodeError: a periodic node must `publish`, take an input, or serve an action; one that does none of them is a timer, and the framework has nothing to offer it
```

**Every rule on this page is checked at decoration**, which is import time: before a
topic is opened and before a release is taken. Rust refuses the same mistakes at compile
time; import is the earliest point Python has.

```python
@periodic(every="20ms", on_overrun=Skip)
```

`every` is the **period**: the time from one release to the next. Releases fall on
`start + n * period`, so they never drift.

`on_overrun` says what happens on an **overrun**, a release whose body runs past the next
release: `Skip`, `CatchUp` or `Fault`, imported from `periodic`. There is no default. The
policies are the Rust ones ([`OverrunPolicy`](periodic_framework_public.md#overrunpolicy)).

```
NodeError: a periodic node must declare `on_overrun`, one of Skip, CatchUp or Fault; there is no default, because a cycle that misses its deadline is a safety-relevant event and silence is not an answer to it
```

A duration is an integer and a unit, `ns`, `us`, `ms` or `s`, with nothing between them
([Durations](periodic_framework_public.md#durations)). A mistyped one is refused at
decoration, naming the key and, for an input, its topic:

```python
lidar=subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after="70 ms")
```

```
NodeError: the `stale_after` of topic 'sensor/range' is '70 ms'; write an integer and one of ns, us, ms, s -- as in "20ms". There is no fractional form: write "1500us", not "1.5ms"
```

Any other key is refused, `safety` among them ([Safety](#safety)).

```python
SENSOR_RANGE = Topic("sensor/range", Range, lane="safe")
```

`lane` is `"kernel"`, `"safe"` or `"fast"`
([Topics and lanes](periodic_framework_public.md#topics-and-lanes) says which to choose).
It has no default. A topic without one can be constructed, and `subscribe` and `publish`
refuse it:

```
NodeError: topic 'sensor/range' needs its lane: where the topic is defined, write Topic('sensor/range', Range, lane="kernel"), or "safe", or "fast". The lane belongs to the topic -- both ends must use the same one -- and it has no default
```

**Define a topic in a module both programs import**, so its two ends cannot be written
differently. Two separate definitions, or one in Python and one in Rust, are compared by
the payload's size and layout identity ([Payloads](#payloads)). A payload with two fields
exchanged is refused.

The lane is not compared. A Python reader that writes `lane="kernel"` for a topic its
Rust writer defines on the safe lane starts and receives nothing, and neither side is told.
The Rust page lists [every lane mismatch](periodic_framework_public.md#topics-and-lanes)
and what it does.

```python
lidar=subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after="70ms")
```

The parameter is one input: the topic, then **`stale_after`**, how old a reading may be
before this node reads it as absent. On every release the body is handed a
[`Cycle`](#cycle) in that parameter. These are the words of the Rust attribute,
`#[subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after = "..")]`, in the one place Python offers beside a
parameter.

- Every input needs both parts. There is no default bound and no node-wide bound.
- Each input has its own bound. Two nodes may read one topic with different bounds.
- At each release the framework reads the clock once and judges every input against its
  own `stale_after` at that one reading, so two inputs never disagree about the time.

| Written | `NodeError` |
|---|---|
| `subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE)` | ``the input on topic 'sensor/range' must declare `stale_after`; without it there is no answer to "is this data still usable", and the node would act on whatever it was last given`` |
| `subscribe("sensor/range", stale_after="70ms")` | `a topic is a definition, not a name: define TOPIC = Topic('sensor/range', YourPayload, lane="safe") once, and write subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after="<duration>")` |
| `subscribe(SENSOR_RANGE, stale_after="70ms", lane="safe")` | ``` `lane` is not an input key: the lane belongs to the topic. Write Topic("some/name", YourPayload, lane="safe") where the topic is defined``` |
| `lidar=SENSOR_RANGE` | ``` `drive` parameter `lidar` names topic 'sensor/range' but not whether the node reads or publishes it: write `lidar=subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after="<duration>")` to read it, or `lidar=publish(TOPIC)` to publish it``` |

**Sizing `stale_after`.** Use the Rust page's rule:

```
stale_after >= (lost publications tolerated + 1) x the publisher's period + this node's period
```

Then move it half a node period off, never onto a multiple of the node's period. `drive.py`
runs every 20 ms and tolerates one lost reading from a 20 ms sensor: `2 x 20 + 20 = 60`,
written `"70ms"`. Nothing checks the rule. A bound shorter than the node's period is
accepted, and makes the input usable only on the release a publication arrives.

The bound is measured from receipt at this node. The data may be older by the gap since the
node's previous release, which is one period unless a release ran late.

**A node reads a topic once.** Two inputs that name one topic are refused, naming both:

```
NodeError: `drive` inputs `front` and `rear` name the same topic 'sensor/range': a node reads a topic once
```

```python
velocity=publish(DRIVE_VELOCITY)
```

The parameter is one output. `publish` takes the topic and nothing else; the lane is the
topic's. On every release the body is handed an `Out` in that parameter:

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `velocity.publish(value)` | Hands the output this release's value, an instance of the topic's payload. A reference is kept, not a copy |
| `velocity.publish(None)`, or no call | Nothing is published on that output at this release |
| a second `velocity.publish(...)` in one release | `ValueError: output 'drive/velocity' was already published at this release; an output carries one publication per release` |

- **Nothing is sent at the call.** When the body returns, every output holding a value is
  packed and published, in the order the outputs are declared. A served action's status
  goes out after them.
- **A body that raises publishes nothing** at that release. The exception leaves `run()`.
- **An output handed nothing publishes nothing.** Its readers go on holding what it last
  published. That is not an overrun.

**A body returns nothing.** The output is the parameter, never the return value. The
first release whose body returns a value stops the node:

```
NodeError: `drive` returned Twist, and a node publishes through its outputs, not its return value. Declare one on a parameter, output=publish(TOPIC), write output.publish(value) where `drive` returned the value, and return nothing
```

**A node publishes a topic once.** Two outputs that name one topic are refused, naming both:

```
NodeError: `drive` outputs `front` and `rear` name the same topic 'drive/velocity': a node publishes a topic once
```

One node may name the same topic as an input and as an output. Each release then reads
what an earlier release published.

**A refused publish does not stop the node.** When the transport refuses a publication,
nothing is raised. The other outputs are still published, and the node goes on. The
sixteenth refusal in a row on one output writes one record to the console:

```
drive: 16 consecutive publishes to drive/state refused (Refused); still trying
```

A publish the transport takes ends the run, and so does a release that hands that output
nothing. A refused value is not sent again. A Rust node writes the same record to its log
ring; a Python node writes it to the console, so `logview` does not show it.

headingPath: What the body may look like
chunks.text:
`run()` calls the body with one argument per parameter, positionally, in the order they
are written: a `Cycle` for an input, an `Out` for an output, the value in force for a
[run-time parameter](#run-time-parameters), the node's `Goal` for a
[served action](#actions). So every parameter must be one of the four.

| Written | `NodeError` |
|---|---|
| `def drive(gain, lidar=subscribe(...))` | ``` `drive` parameter `gain` is not fed by anything. A parameter of a periodic body is an input, `gain=subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after="<duration>")`, an output, `gain=publish(TOPIC)`, a run-time parameter, `gain=param(<default>, range=(<min>, <max>))`, or a served action, `gain=serve(ACTION, lease="<duration>")` ``` |
| `def drive(*readings)` | ``` `drive` takes `*readings`, and a periodic body is called with exactly one argument per declared input or parameter: ...``` |
| `def drive(**options)` | ``` `drive` takes `**options`, and a periodic body is called positionally and is never passed a keyword. Remove `**options` ``` |
| `async def drive(...)` | ``` `drive` is declared `async def`, so calling it would return a coroutine and run nothing. A periodic body is an ordinary function, called once per release; remove `async` ``` |
| a body that contains `yield` | ``` `drive` contains `yield`, so calling it would return a generator and run nothing. ...``` |

- **A method** is declared bound to its object: `periodic(every="10ms",
  on_overrun=Skip)(Estimator().step)`, as in [`Cycle`](#cycle). Its first parameter
  receives the object. `@periodic` on a method inside its class body is refused, with this
  bound form as the fix.
- **A wrapper** made by another decorator, around the function that declares the inputs or
  run-time parameters, is refused: what it wraps declares them, not the wrapper. Put
  `@periodic` directly on the function that declares them.
- **A body called by hand** finds its parameters still holding their declarations. Using
  one as a `Cycle` raises a `NodeError` that says `run()` is what calls a periodic body.

chunks.text:
