**action**: a request that takes many releases, such as "drive to (2.0, 0.5)": a client sends a goal, and the serving node reports feedback on every release and ends it with a result.

**frame (coordinate frame)**: one of the robot's coordinate systems. Frame sets and their lookup are Rust only in this release; a Python node uses the conventions in `tail_messages`.

**goal**: one request of an action, sent by a client and handed to the serving node's body on every release until it ends.

**input**: a topic a node reads, declared on a parameter with `subscribe(TOPIC, stale_after="..")`; the body is handed a `Cycle` there.

**lane**: how a topic's messages travel, written in the topic's definition: `"kernel"` copies through the kernel (up to 4 writers, 4 KiB), `"safe"` shares memory with one writer and may carry safety data, `"fast"` shares memory with one writer and may not.

**layout identity**: a 32-bit hash of a payload's fields, their order and types, which `Payload(..)` computes as the Rust derive does; an end whose identity differs from the topic's is refused at open.

**lease**: how long a served goal lives without its client's keep-alive, at least twice the period, after which the node ends the goal abandoned.

**node**: a function, or a bound method, given to `@periodic(..)`, whose body `run()` calls once on every release.

**output**: a topic a node publishes, declared on a parameter with `publish(TOPIC)`; the body is handed an `Out` there, and what it hands `out.publish(..)` is published when the body returns.

**overrun**: a release that runs past the next one; `on_overrun` says what happens then.

**parameter**: a run-time parameter, a value declared with `param(default, range=(minimum, maximum))` that the shell can change while the node runs.

**payload**: the type a topic carries, a standard `tail_messages` record or your own declared with `Payload("fields", "Name")`.

**period**: the interval `every` sets; releases fall on `start + n * period`.

**release**: one scheduled instant on the period's grid, at which the body runs once.

**release journal**: the record every node that publishes writes on `<function name>/__releases` at every release, which replay reads.

**replay**: running one node again, offline, against a recording, with `--replay FILE` at the end of its command line, and comparing its outputs with the recorded ones.

**stale_after**: an input's bound on how old a sample may be, measured from receipt at this node, before it reads as absent.

**topic**: a named channel that carries one payload type on one lane, defined once with `Topic(name, payload, lane=..)`.

Declare an interface once; the framework generates the typed client every caller uses and the dispatch every server runs. A server is an `impl` block with an attribute — there is no `main`, no receive loop and no reply bookkeeping to write. An **aperiodic service** is a server whose work arrives when something asks for it, not on a clock. Each request goes through the same three steps: the framework **receives** it, **dispatches** it to your handler, and sends **exactly one reply**. A driver that answers "read this pin", a log server that hands out rings, a planner that answers "is this path clear?" are all aperiodic services. Its sibling, the [periodic node](../../periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md), runs a body once per declared period and exchanges data over topics. Use a periodic node for a control loop that runs at a fixed rate. Use an aperiodic service for a question that one caller asks and one server answers, at any time. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: The path of one request accDescr: A caller thread's request is copied by the kernel to the server's receiving thread, decoded with its operation and length checked, handed to your handler, and answered with exactly one reply back to the caller. caller("caller thread
limits.get(..)"):::prog kernel[["kernel
copies the request"]]:::kern receiver{{"receiving thread
of the server"}}:::svc check{{"decode
operation and length checked"}}:::svc handler("your handler
fn get"):::prog reply{{"exactly one reply"}}:::svc caller --> kernel --> receiver --> check --> handler --> reply reply -.-> caller ``` *A caller's request is copied by the kernel to the server's receiving thread, checked and decoded, handed to your handler, and answered with exactly one reply.*

Three files in the BSP's `app/` directory: the interface, defined once, and two programs
that each hold one end of it.

| File | Is |
|---|---|
| `app/speed_limit_interface.rs` | the interface: service name, operations, payloads |
| `app/speed_limit_server/src/main.rs` | the server that holds a speed limit per wheel |
| `app/drive_setup/src/main.rs` | a client that sets one limit and reads it back |

Add `/usr/bin/speed_limit_server=speed_limit_server` and
`/usr/bin/drive_setup=drive_setup` to the `[disk]` section of the BSP's `tail.build`, then
run `./make-disk.sh`. See
[Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](../../../doc/install_rpi3.md#add-your-own-programs).
`aperiodic`, `wire_plain` and `log` are libraries of the SDK, so a program names them with
a `use` and nothing more.

On the booted image, start them in either order: `speed_limit_server &`, then
`drive_setup`. If the client starts first, `connect()` waits for the name.

**In a cargo workspace the interface is a library crate instead**, depending on `aperiodic`
and `wire_plain`; the server and every client list it in their `Cargo.toml`. The server
also lists `log`, because the generated `main` creates its log tag. The interface crate's
public signatures name `ErrorKind` and `CallerIdentity`, which reach it through `std`; put
`#![allow(exported_private_dependencies)]` on the module that declares the trait to silence
the resulting lint.

`#[interface(name = <&str constant>)]` goes on a trait. Every method of the trait is one
operation, and carries `#[op(..)]`:

```rust
#[op(OP_GET, reply = Limit)]
fn get(&self, args: GetLimit) -> Result<Limit, ErrorKind>;
```

| Part | Rule |
|---|---|
| `OP_GET` | the operation number, a `u64` constant. Two operations with the same number fail to build |
| `reply = Limit` | the reply type; `reply = ()` for an operation that answers with nothing |
| `&self` | always `&self`. `&mut self` is refused with a message that says where mutable state goes |
| `args: GetLimit` | the request payload, always present. An operation with nothing to send takes a payload with one reserved field |
| a third parameter `caller: CallerIdentity` | optional: the kernel-stamped identity of the calling process (see [Who is calling](#who-is-calling)) |
| return type | `Result<Reply, ErrorKind>`, matching `reply = ..` |

Further keys on `#[op]`:

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
| `defer` | the handler answers later, through a reply token; see [Deferred replies](#deferred-replies) |
| `trailing` | the request is the payload followed by a run of bytes; see [Bulk data](#bulk-data-trailing) |

A request payload is a `#[repr(C)]` struct that derives `WirePlain`, the same derive the
periodic framework uses for topic payloads. The derive proves at the definition that any
bytes another process sends form a valid value: fields are fixed-width integers, floats,
arrays of them or other such structs, and the struct has no padding. Declare a reply type
the same way: the client builds it from bytes the server sent.

The service checks each request's **length** against the declared payload, and its
operation number against the interface. It does not compare layouts beyond that, so build
both programs from the same interface definition.

| You write | The build says |
|---|---|
| a request payload over 32 bytes | ``request payload `X` exceeds the register fastpath bound (<= 32 bytes)`` |
| a reply type over 32 bytes | ``reply type `X` exceeds the register fastpath bound (<= 32 bytes)`` |
| two operations with one number | `` `b` declares the same discriminant value as `a`; the second is unreachable `` |
| a method without `#[op]` | ``every method of an `#[interface]` trait declares an operation: ..`` |
| a payload that does not derive `WirePlain` | an unsatisfied `WirePlain` bound on the payload |
| `#[aperiodic]` without `tag` | `` `#[aperiodic]` needs the subsystem its records are filed under, .. `` |

A server is a type that implements `Lifecycle` and the interface trait, with
`#[aperiodic(tag = "..")]` on the trait's `impl`. The tag names the subsystem the server's
log records are filed under.

```mermaid flowchart TD accTitle: The order a server starts in accDescr: Lifecycle start builds the handler, before_register maps hardware and spawns threads, the name is registered, after_register publishes other signals, the service ready record is written, and the server then serves requests. start("Lifecycle::start
build the handler"):::prog before("before_register
map hardware, spawn threads"):::prog register{{"the name is registered"}}:::svc after("after_register
publish other signals"):::prog ready{{"record: service ready"}}:::svc serve{{"serve requests"}}:::svc start --> before --> register --> after --> ready --> serve ``` *The handler is built, prepared before its name exists, registered, given a step after registration, announced as ready, and then serves.* | Hook | Runs | Use it for | |---|---|---| | `fn start(log: LogTag) -> Result` | first, before anything is logged or registered | building the handler. Required | | `fn before_register(&mut self, log: LogTag) -> Result<(), Unavailable>` | before the name exists, so no client can reach the service | mapping hardware, attaching interrupts, spawning helper threads. Default: nothing | | `fn after_register(&mut self, log: LogTag) -> Result<(), Unavailable>` | after the name exists; clients that arrive now wait in the queue | publishing a second readiness signal that must not appear before the name. Default: nothing | A hook stops start-up by returning an error: | Returned | Recorded | The process | |---|---|---| | `Err(ErrorKind)` from `start` | `startup failed: `, at error | exits 1; the name is never registered | | `Err(Unavailable::Failed(kind))` | `startup failed: `, at error | exits 1 | | `Err(Unavailable::NotPresent)` | `not present on this board`, at info | exits 0: a board without the device is not a fault | `?` works inside a hook on any `Result<_, ErrorKind>`: an `ErrorKind` converts into `Unavailable::Failed`. The hooks take `&mut self`. The handler methods take `&self`, and the handler type must be `Sync`, because it is shared with the thread that receives requests. Keep state you set up once in plain fields; put state that requests change behind a `Mutex` or atomics, as the quick start's `AtomicU32` limits are.

Each service is served by one receiving thread, so its handler runs one request at a time.
While a handler works, every other caller of that service waits. A handler that must wait
for something slow — a device, an event, another program's action — **defers** its reply
instead of blocking.

`LogTag` is `Copy`. Keep the one `start` receives in a field and log through it:

```rust
self.log.warning(format_args!("wheel {} limit cut to {}", args.wheel, args.max_mrad_s));
```

Its levels are `start`, `success`, `info`, `warning`, `error` and `trace`. Records go to the
process's log ring under the server's tag, alongside the framework's own; read them with
`logview`.

An operation that declares a third parameter `caller: CallerIdentity` receives the calling
process's identity. The kernel stamps it, so a client cannot claim to be another process.

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `caller.pid()` | the process id, for looking a process up or logging |
| `caller.generation()` | which occupant of that process slot this is |

Key per-client state on the whole `CallerIdentity`, not on `pid()`. A pid is a reused slot:
state keyed on it alone passes to whatever process takes the slot next, while an identity
does not match a later process. `CallerIdentity` is `Copy`, `Eq` and `Hash`, and prints as
`pid 7 gen 1`.

| Constructor | Waits for the name |
|---|---|
| `SpeedLimitClient::connect()` | up to 100 attempts, 20 ms apart: at most about 2 s |
| `SpeedLimitClient::connect_bounded(attempts, backoff)` | `attempts` times, `backoff` apart; `connect_bounded(1, Duration::ZERO)` checks once and never sleeps |

Both return `Err(NotFound)` when the name is still not registered. The client is `Copy`:
connect once and hand a copy to each thread that calls.

A call has **no timeout**. It returns when the server answers or when the server's process
ends. Design a service so that every request is answered: answer at once, or defer and
answer when the awaited event happens or is abandoned.

A request is served at the caller's priority. When the kernel hands a request to the
receiving thread it raises that thread to at least the caller's priority, and it ends the
raise at the reply. An idle receiving thread runs at the default thread priority, 31. A
high-priority caller is therefore not served at a lower server's priority, and a server
need not be started at the priority of its most urgent client.

Every error is an `ErrorKind`, carried unchanged from where it arose:

| `Err(..)` | Means |
|---|---|
| the kind the handler returned | the server refused the request: `InvalidInput`, `ResourceBusy`, `PermissionDenied`, or any other kind it chose |
| `NotFound` | from `connect`: the name was not registered in time. From a call: the service ended before answering — its process exited or crashed |
| `Unsupported` | the server has no such operation: the two programs were built from different interface versions |
| `InvalidInput` | the request's length is not the declared payload's: likewise a version mismatch, unless the handler returned it |
| `ConnectionAborted` | the server dropped the token for this deferred request |
| `WouldBlock` | the service already has 16 requests waiting, or a message over 256 bytes found no free buffer in the kernel's message pool. Nothing was done; the call may be repeated |
| `ArgumentListTooLong` | the request is longer than the server accepts (see [Message sizes](#message-sizes)) |

A panic in a handler ends the server process. Every caller waiting on it receives
`NotFound`.

| Message | Limit | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| a request payload | 32 bytes | at build time |
| a reply value | 32 bytes | at build time |
| a `trailing` request: payload plus bytes | 256 KiB | at the call: `ArgumentListTooLong` |

The kernel carries a message of up to 32 bytes in registers. Up to 256 bytes it copies the
message through the two threads' own buffers, which no other traffic can exhaust. A longer
message travels through a shared message pool of 4 KiB, 64 KiB and 256 KiB buffers, so
only messages over 256 bytes can meet the pool's `WouldBlock`.

An operation declared `trailing` carries a fixed payload followed by any number of bytes.
The handler takes them as its next parameter:

```rust
#[op(OP_WRITE, reply = Written, trailing)]
fn write(&self, args: WriteHeader, data: &[u8]) -> Result<Written, ErrorKind>;
```

The generated client method takes the bytes beside the payload and returns the reply as
bytes, which `aperiodic::decode` turns back into the reply type:

```rust
let bytes = storage.write(WriteHeader { handle, data_len: block.len() as u64 }, &block)?;
let written: Written = aperiodic::decode(&bytes)?;
```

A service with a `trailing` operation gives its receiving thread a 256 KiB request buffer,
because such a request may be that long. A service without one sizes the buffer to its
largest declared payload.

`#[aperiodic(tag = "..", no_main)]` generates everything but `main`. Your own `main` then
does its own preparation and ends in `aperiodic::run::<StatusService>(log::log_tag!("status"))`,
which never returns.

To serve a second service in the same process, give it a thread of its own.
`aperiodic::bind::<H>(log)` builds and registers one service and returns a `Bound<H>`;
`aperiodic::serve(bound)` serves it for good. A `Bound` cannot move between threads, so bind
and serve on the same thread. A process registers at most 16 services; a seventeenth bind
fails with `OutOfMemory`, and registering a name that is already taken fails with
`AlreadyExists`.

An interface may instead be declared as an enum, one variant per operation. Device drivers
that match on the request directly use this form:

```rust
#[interface(name = BEEPER_SERVICE)]
pub enum BeeperRequest {
    #[op(OP_BEEP, reply = ())]
    Beep(BeepArgs),
}
```

It generates `BeeperClient` with `connect()` and `beep(BeepArgs)`. The server implements
`aperiodic::Handler`, whose `dispatch(&self, request: BeeperRequest, client: ClientId) ->
Outcome` matches on the decoded enum and answers through the `ClientId` exactly as a
deferring operation does. Its `main` names the service at run time:

```rust
fn main() -> ! {
    aperiodic::run_instance(BEEPER_SERVICE, log::log_tag!("beeper"), Dispatcher::new(Beeper::new()))
}
```

The enum form also accepts `#[op(.., pool = MAX)]` for an operation whose reply is longer
than 32 bytes: the payload type implements `aperiodic::FramedRequest`, the handler answers
with `Reply::framed::<Op>(header, tail)`, and the client method takes and returns bytes, at
most `MAX` and never more than 256 KiB.

- **Exactly one reply per request** while the server lives. A handler's `Ok` and `Err`, a
  decode failure, an unknown operation and every ending of a reply token each send one
  reply. Answering twice does not compile.
- **The name appears only when the server is ready.** No client reaches the service before
  `before_register` has returned. A client that arrives during `after_register` waits in
  the queue.
- **A request is checked before your code sees it.** An unknown operation is answered
  `Unsupported` and a payload of the wrong length `InvalidInput`, without calling the
  handler.
- **A dead server releases its callers.** When the server process ends, for any reason,
  every waiting caller returns `NotFound`.
- **The caller's identity is the kernel's**, never a value the client sent.

- **Do not block in a handler.** The service's other callers wait behind it. Defer the
  reply, and answer when the event happens.
- **Do not call your own service from its handler**, directly or through another service
  that calls back: the only receiving thread is busy with you, and the call never returns.
- **Do not drop a reply token to cancel.** Call `abandon(kind)`. A dropped token answers
  `ConnectionAborted` and logs a server bug.
- **Do not hold more tokens than you have bounded.** Refuse past your limit with an error
  reply, as the start gate does with `ResourceBusy`.
- **Do not key ownership on `pid()`.** Use the whole `CallerIdentity`.
- **Do not mix interface versions.** Rebuild every program that uses an interface when the
  interface changes.

Say which device you want by its class and the name the board gave it; the framework finds the driver, checks your request against what the device can do, and carries it there. An application never names a process, a register, a pin-mux code or a wire format. The framework has two tiers: - **The class tier**, one crate per device class: `tail_device_gpio`, `tail_device_i2c`, `tail_device_pwm` and `tail_device_stepper`. Each holds the class's vocabulary (its values, its errors, its capability record), the application's handle types, and the trait a driver of that class implements. An application and a driver each name only their class crate. - **The core tier**, `tail_device_core`, is what every driver needs whatever its class: the board's resources for the driver, a mapped register window, and the interrupt path. Applications never touch it, and a driver reaches it through its class crate. Every driver is an ordinary user-space process. It is started by the board's image manifest, told its registers and interrupts on its startup line, and advertises itself under an **instance name** the board assigns: `gpio-lines`, `sensor-bus`, `pwm-channels`, `drive-motors`. Each class crate exports those names as constants, so an application writes `gpio::LINES`, never a string and never a board fact. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: Device instances and what each one uses accDescr: An application opens gpio-lines, sensor-bus, pwm-channels and drive-motors by name. The stepper driver behind drive-motors uses pwm-channels and gpio-lines; the PWM and I2C drivers use gpio-lines for their pins. app("your application"):::prog lines[/"gpio-lines
(gpio_rpi3)"\]:::hw bus[/"sensor-bus
(i2c_rpi3)"\]:::hw pwmc[/"pwm-channels
(pwm_rpi3)"\]:::hw motors[/"drive-motors
(stepper_step_dir)"\]:::hw app --> lines app --> bus app --> pwmc app --> motors motors --> pwmc motors --> lines pwmc --> lines bus --> lines ``` *An application opens instances by name; the stepper driver drives its motors through the PWM and GPIO instances, and the PWM and I2C drivers take their pins from the GPIO instance.*

The class crates are libraries of the SDK: a program in the BSP's `app/` directory names
them with `use` and nothing more (see
[Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3](../../../doc/install_rpi3.md#add-your-own-programs)).

| Class | Open | Instance constant | Name |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPIO | `Gpio::open(gpio::LINES)` | `tail_device_gpio::gpio::LINES` | `gpio-lines` |
| I2C | `I2c::open(i2c::SENSOR_BUS)` | `tail_device_i2c::i2c::SENSOR_BUS` | `sensor-bus` |
| PWM | `Pwm::open(pwm::CHANNELS)` | `tail_device_pwm::pwm::CHANNELS` | `pwm-channels` |
| Stepper | `Stepper::open(stepper::DRIVE_MOTORS)` | `tail_device_stepper::stepper::DRIVE_MOTORS` | `drive-motors` |

- **`open` waits for the driver.** If the instance is not advertised yet, `open` retries
  for about two seconds (100 attempts, 20 ms apart). If it never appears, it fails with
  `DriverGone`, so a program can start before its drivers without a retry loop of its own.
- **The capability record is fetched once, at open.** `capabilities()` on the handle makes
  no call. Each class checks a request against it before sending, so a request the device
  cannot honour fails locally with the reason (`Unsupported`, `OutOfRange`,
  `TooManySegments { max }` and so on).
- **A handle does not re-resolve.** If the driver exits after a successful open, the next
  call fails with `DriverGone` or `Transport(..)`.
- Error enums are `#[non_exhaustive]`: give a `match` on one a default arm. A status the
  build does not know arrives as `Unknown { code }`.

A `Gpio` is an opened bank of lines; a `GpioLine` is your claim on one line.

| Acquire | Gives you |
|---|---|
| `gpio.output(line, level)` | an output, driven to `level` from its first edge |
| `gpio.input(line, bias)` | an input with `Bias::PullUp`, `PullDown` or `Disabled` |
| `gpio.input_watching(line, edges)` | an input already armed for `EdgeMask::RISING`, `FALLING` or both (`RISING \| FALLING`) |
| `gpio.board_function(line)` | the line handed to the peripheral the board wired it for; you never name an alternate-function number |
| `gpio.lines(&selectors, config)` | several lines with one `PinConfig`, all or none |

| On a `GpioLine` | Does |
|---|---|
| `set_high()`, `set_low()`, `set_level(level)` | drive an output; on a line that is not an output, `InvalidRequest` |
| `level()` | sample the line |
| `configure(config)` | apply every field of a `PinConfig` that is not `Unchanged` |
| `watch(edges)`, `disarm()` | arm or disarm edge detection |
| `wait_edge()` | block until an armed edge arrives; returns an `EdgeEvent { line, edges, .. }` |

```rust
use tail_device_gpio::{gpio, EdgeMask, Gpio};

/// An emergency-stop button on GPIO27, pulling the line low when pressed.
const ESTOP: u32 = 27;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let gpio = Gpio::open(gpio::LINES)?;
    let estop = gpio.input_watching(ESTOP, EdgeMask::FALLING)?;
    loop {
        let event = estop.wait_edge()?;
        println!("e-stop pressed on line {}", event.line);
    }
}
```

Arming inside the acquire means no edge can fall between claiming the line and arming it.

Things to know:

- **Lines are addressed by number.** `LineSelector` also accepts a name, but board line
  names are not resolved yet: a name fails with `UnknownLine` on every board.
- **Edges report the armed mask, not the direction**, on `gpio_rpi3`
  (`capabilities().event_reports_direction` is 0). Sample `level()` if you need the
  direction. QEMU does not emulate GPIO edge interrupts, so `wait_edge` waits forever
  there; it works on the board.
- A bias takes effect when `configure` returns, but a line with a capacitive load reaches
  it only as fast as the load allows. Let it settle before sampling or arming.
- `gpio_rpi3` supports bias; it has no programmable drive strength or polarity, so a
  `PinConfig` asking for either fails `Unsupported`.
- Releasing or disarming a line cancels a `wait_edge` parked on it with `Cancelled`.

| `GpioError` | Means |
|---|---|
| `UnknownLine` | no such line on this instance |
| `InUse` | another process holds the line, or the line is a driver's (see [Ownership](#ownership)) |
| `Reserved` | the system holds the line (the serial console's GPIO14/15) |
| `NotOwner` | you operated a line you do not hold |
| `Unsupported`, `InvalidRequest` | the instance cannot apply the configuration, or the request is wrong for the line's role |
| `WaiterCapacity`, `Cancelled` | too many parked waits; a wait cancelled by release or disarm |
| `DriverGone`, `Transport(..)` | the driver is not there, or the call itself failed |

An `I2c` is an opened bus. A transaction is atomic: its segments run back to back with a
repeated START between them, and no other client's transaction runs in between. Clients
need no lock and no claim; the driver queues and serializes them.

| On an `I2c` | Does |
|---|---|
| `write(address, &bytes)` | one write |
| `read::<N>(address)` | one read of `N` bytes, returned as `[u8; N]` |
| `write_read::<N>(address, &command)` | write then read, as one transaction |
| `transaction()` | build a transaction of up to 8 segments: `.write(..)`, `.read(address, len)`, then `.execute()` returns the read bytes as a `Vec<u8>` |
| `set_bus_speed(hz)` | set the bus clock; returns the rate actually achieved. It applies to every client of the bus |

`N` is inferred from the binding (`let bytes: [u8; 6] = bus.read(IMU)?;`). An address
written as a `u8` is a 7-bit address; `I2cAddress::ten_bit(0x123)?` is the 10-bit form,
and `I2cAddress::seven_bit(0xD0)` fails `AddressOutOfRange { max: 0x7F }` rather than
silently addressing another device. `i2c_rpi3` supports 7-bit addresses, standard and
fast mode, one read segment per transaction (and it must be last), and one device
address per transaction.

On QEMU the emulated controller has no repeated START, so `write_read` and any
multi-segment transaction fail with `AtomicityLost { segments_completed: 1 }`. There,
use a `write` followed by a `read` as two transactions.

| `I2cError` | Means | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| `Nack { phase, bytes_transferred }` | the device did not acknowledge | unchanged only if `bytes_transferred == 0` |
| `Timeout { .. }`, `ClockStretchTimeout { .. }` | the transfer missed the driver's deadline, or the device held the clock too long | same rule |
| `AtomicityLost { segments_completed }` | the bus was released between segments, so part of it ran | never unchanged: re-read the device's state first |
| `BusInUse` | the driver's queue is full | yes, immediately |
| `BusBusy`, `ArbitrationLost` | the wire is busy, or another master won | yes |
| `Unsupported`, `AddressOutOfRange`, `TooManySegments`, `PayloadTooLarge`, `Malformed` | the transaction cannot run on this instance | fix the request |
| `ShortRead`, `DriverGone`, `Transport(..)` | the driver answered short, is gone, or the call failed | — |

A `Stepper` drives every motor of an instance at once. `drive-motors` is a differential
drive with two motors, **motor 0 the left wheel and motor 1 the right**, seen from behind.

```rust
use tail_device_stepper::{stepper, StepRate, Stepper};

let motors = Stepper::open(stepper::DRIVE_MOTORS)?;
let forward = StepRate::from_full_steps_per_second(100.0);
let [left, right] = motors.drive([forward, forward])?; // the rates actually emitted
// ... one drive per control cycle ...
motors.disable()?; // stop and de-energize now, not when the lease runs out
```

- **The lease.** Each `drive` is valid for `capabilities().lease_ms` (between 2 and 500 ms,
  set by the board). If no fresh `drive` arrives in time, the class disables every motor
  itself. Another process is refused with `InUse` while the lease is live.
- **Every lease starts from rest.** The first `drive` of a lease emits zero on every motor;
  later ones are clamped to the instance's maximum rate, limited by its acceleration, and
  floored to zero below its minimum rate. The returned array says what was emitted.
- **No enable, direction or claim to manage.** The class enables the motors while a lease
  is live and sets direction from the sign of each rate.
- The array length must equal `capabilities().motor_count`, or `drive` fails
  `WrongMotorCount` without a call. `full_steps_per_revolution` in the same record turns
  a wheel speed into a rate.

`StepperError`: `WrongMotorCount`, `InUse`, `NotOwner` (a `disable` while another process
holds the lease), `Hardware` (an output did not take the setting: the lease is ended and
the motors disabled), `DriverGone`, `Transport(..)`.

headingPath: Using a device from a periodic node

chunks.text:
| Class | Who may use it | How it ends |
|---|---|---|
| GPIO | one process per line, from claim to release; a second claim, even from the same process, is `InUse` | `GpioLine` dropped. Lines held by a process that exits are released when another process next claims one of them; **until then they keep their level** |
| I2C | every process; transactions are serialized | nothing to end |
| PWM | the process whose `apply` took the channel | `stop`, or the hold passing without a refresh |
| Stepper | the process whose `drive` took the lease | `disable`, or the lease passing without a `drive` |

Drivers claim lines from `gpio-lines` like any other client, so on a Raspberry Pi 3 GPIO2
and GPIO3 belong to `i2c_rpi3` and GPIO18 and GPIO19 to `pwm_rpi3`, and a claim on them is
`InUse`. GPIO14 and GPIO15 carry the serial console and are always `Reserved`. A released
or reclaimed line is left driving nothing.

headingPath: What is portable and what is the board's
chunks.text:
Your application depends on the **class**: its crate, its instance names and its
capability record. Which chip sits behind an instance, which pins it uses and what its
limits are is the **board's**, written once on the driver's line in the image manifest.
These are the Raspberry Pi 3 lines:

```text
gpio_rpi3 base=0x3F200000 size=0x1000 irq=49,50,51 instance=gpio-lines altmap=2:4,3:4,18:2,19:2,...
pwm_rpi3  base=0x3F20C000 size=0x1000 clock=0x3F101000 lines=18,19 instance=pwm-channels
i2c_rpi3  base=0x3F804000 size=0x1000 irq=53 core_clock_hz=250000000 lines=2,3 instance=sensor-bus
```

| Instance | Driver | Board image | QEMU image |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpio-lines` | `gpio_rpi3`: the BCM2837's 54 lines | started | started; no edge interrupts |
| `sensor-bus` | `i2c_rpi3`: BSC1 on GPIO2 (SDA) and GPIO3 (SCL) | started | started; no repeated START |
| `pwm-channels` | `pwm_rpi3`: channel 0 on GPIO18, channel 1 on GPIO19 | started | not started: QEMU models no PWM |
| `drive-motors` | `stepper_step_dir`: STEP from `pwm-channels`, DIR and ENABLE from `gpio-lines` | packed, not started | not started |

`stepper_step_dir` has no registers of its own, so it runs on any board that has a PWM and
a GPIO instance. It is not started by default because its pins belong to a stepper HAT
that may not be fitted. An image for a robot with one adds a line like:

```text
stepper_step_dir step_channels=1,0 dir_lines=13,24 dir_inverted=0,1 enable_lines=12,4
    enable_active=high microsteps=16 full_steps_per_revolution=200
    max_rate_full_steps_per_s=1250 min_rate_full_steps_per_s=32
    max_acceleration_full_steps_per_s2=10000 step_pulse_ns=2500 lease_ms=6
    instance=drive-motors
```

(one line in the manifest; wrapped here). Motor `i` is the `i`-th entry of each list, and
the driver refuses a line whose lists disagree, exiting before the name is advertised.

headingPath: Writing a driver for a new board

chunks.text:
Four programs on the target shell (`tsh`) show what a running robot application is doing,
without changing a line of it:

| Tool | Answers |
|---|---|
| [`topic`](#topic) | Which topics exist, how fast are they published, what do they carry? Record them, print a recording, play it back. |
| [`node`](#node) | Which periodic nodes are running, and how is each one declared? |
| [`param`](#param) | What are a node's run-time parameters, and set them while it runs. |
| [`logview`](#logview) | What did each program write to the system log, including programs that have exited? |

They work the same for nodes written in Rust and in Python: each node announces itself,
journals its releases and serves its parameters through the framework, so the tools see
every node alike.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: What each shell tool reads from a node
  accDescr: A periodic node publishes its topics, read by topic; its description, read by node; and its parameters, read by param, which also writes requests back to the node. The node's log ring is read by logview.
  N("periodic node"):::prog
  T("topic")
  D("node")
  P("param")
  L("logview")
  N -->|"its topics"| T
  N -->|"node/__node"| D
  N -->|"node/__params"| P
  P -->|"node/__param_set"| N
  N -->|"log ring"| L
```

*A node publishes its topics, its description and its parameters; `topic`, `node` and
`param` read them, `param` also writes a request back, and `logview` reads the node's log
ring.*

Every tool prints `usage: ...` and exits 2 on a malformed command line, and exits 1 with a
one-line reason on standard error when it cannot do what was asked. Output examples on this
page are illustrative: process ids, counts and layout identities differ on your system.

```text
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &
tsh> node list
brake  pid 9   brake
drive  pid 10  drive
lidar  pid 8   lidar
tsh> topic list
brake/__node        kernel   1 writer    0/8 readers       96 B   layout 0x...
brake/__releases    kernel   1 writer    0/8 readers      120 B   layout 0x...
cmd/velocity        kernel   1 writer    1/8 readers       48 B   Twist
sensor/range        safe     1 writer    1/8 readers       32 B   Range
...
tsh> topic hz -n 3 sensor/range
# times are when topic saw each publication (1 ms poll); they may not match the publisher's timing
average rate: 50.00 Hz   min: 19.0 ms   max: 21.0 ms   window: 50
average rate: 50.00 Hz   min: 19.0 ms   max: 21.0 ms   window: 50
average rate: 50.00 Hz   min: 19.0 ms   max: 21.0 ms   window: 50
tsh> topic echo -n 1 cmd/velocity
# cmd/velocity: kernel lane, Twist, 48 B, layout 0x...
linear.x=0.5 linear.y=0 linear.z=0 angular.x=0 angular.y=0 angular.z=-0.25
```

The topics ending in `/__node`, `/__releases`, `/__params` and `/__param_set` belong to
the framework: a node's description, its release journal and its parameter channel. They
are listed like any other topic.

```text
usage: topic list
       topic hz     [-n REPORTS] [--lane kernel|safe|fast] NAME
       topic echo   [-n COUNT]   [--lane kernel|safe|fast] [--as "DECL"] NAME
       topic record [-o PATH] [-d SECONDS] [NAME...]
       topic dump   FILE [--topic NAME] [-n COUNT]
       topic play   FILE [-r RATE] [-s SECONDS] NAME...
```

`topic COMMAND --help` prints the full description of one command.

One line per topic on every lane, sorted by name: the name, the lane (`kernel`, `safe` or
`fast`), its writers, its readers out of its reader capacity, its payload size, and its
type. The type is a standard payload's name (`Twist`, `Range`, `Odometry`, ...) when the
topic's layout identity and size match one, and `layout 0x...` otherwise.

Listing opens nothing and changes no count. The counts can over-report:

- a running `topic hz` or `topic echo` is an ordinary reader, and is counted as one;
- a fast-lane reader, or a safe- or fast-lane writer, that dropped its end stays counted
  until its process exits.

Measures the rate a topic is published at and prints one report a second:

```text
average rate: 50.00 Hz   min: 19.0 ms   max: 21.0 ms   window: 50
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `window` | publications in the last second, counted from the publisher's own sequence numbers, so exact even for publications the poll did not see |
| `average rate` | `window` divided by the time between the two observations that bound it |
| `min`, `max` | shortest and longest gap between two consecutive publications the poll saw; `n/a` when every change it saw spanned several publications |
| `not seen` | publications counted in the window that the poll did not see one by one |

`hz` reads as one ordinary reader, polling every 1 ms at the lowest priority. Its times are
when it saw each publication, not when the publisher published it, which is what its first
line says: under load `max` grows and a rate can read low, but `window` stays exact.
`no new messages` is printed for a second with nothing new.

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `-n REPORTS` | exit 0 after REPORTS reports; without it, `hz` runs until stopped |
| `--lane LANE` | read NAME on this lane, when a topic of that name exists on more than one |

`hz` exits 1 when the topic has no writer, or once its writer is gone.

Prints a topic's payloads as `field=value` pairs. The first line names the lane, the type,
the size and the layout identity. `echo` polls every 10 ms and prints the newest
publication it has not printed yet; publications it skipped are counted on a line of their
own, `# missed N`.

A payload is decoded by the first of these that applies:

1. `--as "DECL"`: a declaration in the Python `Payload` grammar, used only when its layout
   identity and size equal the topic's. Otherwise `echo` says why and prints hex.
   ```text
   tsh> topic echo --as "stamp:u64 range_mm:u32 quality:u32" lidar/raw
   tsh> topic echo --as "linear:Vector3 angular:Vector3" cmd/velocity
   ```
2. A standard payload of `robot_messages`, found by layout identity and size.
3. Hex: the first 256 bytes and the total length.

`-n COUNT` exits 0 after COUNT printed publications; `--lane` is as for `hz`. `echo` exits
1 when the topic has no writer, or once its writer is gone.

Records every publication of every topic on every lane, or of the topics named, into an
[MCAP](https://mcap.dev) file, each with its lane sequence number and the time it was read.
Standard MCAP tools on a development host can open the file.

```text
tsh> topic record -o /recordings/run7.mcap &        start it BEFORE the nodes
recording to /recordings/run7.mcap
tsh> lidar & brake & drive &
```

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `-o PATH` | write PATH, which must not exist. Without it: the next `/recordings/run<N>.mcap`, the directory created if absent |
| `-d SECONDS` | stop after SECONDS, write each topic's counts and the file's footer, and exit 0. Without it, `record` runs until stopped, and the file is readable up to its last whole record |

- **Start `record` before the nodes.** A kernel-lane topic hands a late reader only the
  newest 8 publications it still holds, and replaying a node needs its journal from its
  first release.
- **Nothing is lost silently.** A topic `record` cannot attach to (every reader seat taken,
  or a payload over 65489 bytes) is in the file with the reason and named on standard
  error. A publication overwritten before it was read is a gap in its topic's sequence,
  which `topic dump` reports.
- `record` reads at priority 30, below every node, polls every 1 ms and looks for new
  topics every 100 ms. It exits 1 if PATH exists, or as soon as a write fails or the disk is
  full, saying how many bytes the file holds.

Prints a recording: its time base, each topic where it first appears, and each
publication as

```text
RECEIPT_NS seq SEQUENCE NAME: field=value ...
```

Standard payloads are decoded; anything else is printed as hex, with the reason on its
topic's line. Every sequence number from 1 to the last one read is either a record or
accounted for on a line of its own:

```text
# sensor/range: 12 before the recording (seq 1..12)
# sensor/range: missed 3 (seq 140..142)
# sensor/range: missed 1 after the last record (seq 2104..2104)
```

`--topic NAME` prints one topic only; `-n COUNT` stops after COUNT records.

Publishes again what a recording holds for the topics named: each payload byte for byte,
on its recorded topic name and lane, at its recorded distance from the first one played.

```text
tsh> topic play /recordings/run7.mcap sensor/range
playing sensor/range  safe  32 B  Range
sensor/range  safe  2104 published  0 skipped  worst lateness 0.412 ms
```

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `-r RATE` | publish RATE times as fast, e.g. `0.5` or `2`; default 1. Only the data's pace changes, never a node's period |
| `-s SECONDS` | start SECONDS into the recording; earlier records are counted as skipped |

- At least one topic must be named; `topic dump FILE` lists what a recording holds.
- `play` refuses a topic that already has a live writer: stop the node that publishes it
  first. This is how a node is fed its recorded inputs live, with the real sensors off.
- A record is never published early and never skipped: one found late is published at
  once, and the summary reports each topic's worst lateness.
- At `-r 0.5`, an input whose `stale_after` is under twice the topic's period reads stale on
  some releases; at `-r 2`, a node misses publications. That is the data's pace changing,
  not a fault.

Replaying a node is not a `topic` command: the node itself does it, from a recording, when
`--replay FILE` ends its command line. It runs the node's body once per recorded release
against exactly what that release was handed, and compares the outputs:

```text
tsh> brake --replay /recordings/run7.mcap
replay: brake life 1: 2104 releases, 2103 compared, identical
tsh> python steer.py --replay /recordings/run7.mcap
```

The periodic framework guides explain it in full:
[Rust](../../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md#recording-and-replay),
[Python](../../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md#recording-and-replay).

```text
usage: node list | node info NODE
```

Every periodic node, Rust or Python, announces itself when it starts. `node` reads those
announcements; the node does nothing extra for it.

```text
tsh> node list
balance  pid 7  balance
tsh> node info balance
balance
  Process: pid 7 (balance), thread 0
  Period: 5ms, on_overrun Skip
  Priority: 31
  Subscribers:
    imu/data: safe, stale_after 12ms
  Publishers:
    motor/command: kernel
  Action Servers:
  Parameters: 2, settable
```

`node list` prints one line per running node: its name, its process id and its program.
`node info` prints, for each running node of that name, its process and thread, its period
and overrun policy, its priority when it started, every input with its lane and
`stale_after`, every output with its lane, the actions it serves, and how many run-time
parameters it has.

- A node that has stopped is not listed.
- A node replaying a recording announces nothing, so it is not listed.
- Two running nodes with one name are both listed, with a warning: node names should be
  unique within an image.
- If the image's topic storage is full, a node runs unlisted and says so once in its log:
  `brake: no node description (topic storage full); node list does not show this node`.

```text
usage: param list [NODE] | param set NODE NAME VALUE [NAME VALUE...]
```

Lists and sets the run-time parameters a node declares, such as a controller's gains,
while it runs.

```text
tsh> param list
balance  2 parameters
tsh> param list balance
kp = 42.0  (0.0 .. 200.0)
kd = 1.5   (0.0 .. 20.0)
tsh> param set balance kp 45.5
balance: kp = 45.5 from release 18342
tsh> param list balance
kp = 45.5  (0.0 .. 200.0, default 42.0)
kd = 1.5   (0.0 .. 20.0)
tsh> param set balance kp 250
param: balance kp = 250.0 is outside 0.0 .. 200.0; nothing was set
```

- **A set takes effect at the start of a release.** The release `param set` names is the
  first whose body sees the new value; a body never sees a value change while it runs.
- **Set coupled values in one command.** `param set balance kp 50 kd 2.5` is one request,
  applied whole at one release. Two commands are two requests, and at least one release
  runs between them with the new `kp` and the old `kd`.
- **The node checks every request** against its declared ranges, both ends included. A
  value outside its range, a NaN, or an unknown name is refused, and nothing changes.
- `param set` succeeds only on the node's own answer. It exits 1 with what was refused, or
  when the node does not answer within eight of its periods plus 250 ms.
- **Values last for the node's life.** A restart starts at the defaults again; `param list`
  shows each changed value beside its default, so you can copy it into the source.
- **Each applied change is logged** by `param` in its own log ring:
  `balance: kp 42.0 -> 45.5 from release 18342`. Read it with `logview -s param`.
- `param list` names only nodes that declare parameters; `node list` names every node. A
  node declared `safety` has no run-time parameters.

How a node declares parameters:
[Rust](../../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md#run-time-parameters),
[Python](../../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_python_public.md#run-time-parameters).

```text
usage: logview [-s <ring>] [-l <level>] [-f]
       logview console <all|info|status|warning|error|none>
```

Each process that logs has a log ring of its own, in memory shared with the log server.
Writing a record costs no system call; `logview` reads the rings directly and prints
their records merged by time stamp. A ring stays readable after its process exits, so the
last words of a crashed program are still there.

```text
tsh> logview
logview: 5 ring(s)
  brake            pid=9      1 page(s) live
  param            pid=14     1 page(s) dead
  ...
tsh> logview -s brake -l warning
tsh> logview -f
```

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `-s RING` | only rings whose name starts with RING: `-s wifi` matches `wifi_rpi3` |
| `-l LEVEL` | only records at LEVEL or worse: `trace`, `info`, `status` (also `start`, `success`), `warning`, `error` |
| `-f` | follow: keep printing new records until stopped |
| `console LEVEL` | set which records the log server also prints to the console: `all`, `info`, `status` (the default: the boot narrative and anything worse), `warning`, `error` or `none` |

If records were overwritten in a ring before `logview` read them, it says how many.

What lands where:

- A Rust program writes records with `log!(INFO, "...")`. The periodic framework writes a
  Rust node's own reports (a refused publish, a missing journal) to the node's ring, so
  `logview -s <node>` shows them.
- A Python node reports a run of refused publishes on the console, not in a log ring, so
  `logview` does not show it.
- `param` logs every applied change in its ring, `param`.

Try TAIL OS on your Linux machine in under two minutes — no hardware, no
toolchain. For installing TAIL OS on real Raspberry Pi 3 hardware, see
[Installing on Raspberry Pi 3](install_rpi3.md).

| Item | Install command |
|------|-----------------|
| Linux host (Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 tested) | — |
| `qemu-system-aarch64` | `sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils` |
| `curl` or `wget` | usually preinstalled |

That's it. Everything else is bundled in the prebuilt images.

Download the launcher, then run it:

```bash
curl -O https://tail-os.com/downloads/run_tailos_qemu.sh
chmod +x run_tailos_qemu.sh
./run_tailos_qemu.sh
```

The launcher will:

1. Check that QEMU is installed.
2. Download `tail_qemu.rfs` (kernel) and `tail_disk.img` (data disk) into
   `~/.cache/tailos/`, verifying each against the published `SHA256SUMS`. Later runs
   reuse the cache until a new image is published.
3. Boot TAIL OS in QEMU with the correct flags.

When you see `/$`, the system is ready. Exit QEMU with **Ctrl-A, then lowercase x**. Booting it
again is `./run_tailos_qemu.sh`: it starts from the cached images.

```
/$ help
/$ pwd
/$ ls /usr/bin
/$ /usr/bin/ps
/$ cd /usr/bin
/usr/bin$ exit
```

The prompt shows the current directory (it changes after `cd`). The shell also
supports arrow-key history, per-process `cwd`, and background jobs
with `&`.

`exit` ends the shell, and no new one starts: nothing runs and no prompt returns, though
what you type still echoes. Quit QEMU with **Ctrl-A, then lowercase x**.

If you prefer not to run a remote script, do it by hand:

```bash
# 1. Install QEMU
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils

# 2. Download the images, unpack them, and check them
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_qemu.rfs.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/tail_disk.img.gz
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
gunzip tail_qemu.rfs.gz tail_disk.img.gz
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

# 3. Boot
qemu-system-aarch64 \
    -M raspi3b \
    -kernel tail_qemu.rfs \
    -serial mon:stdio \
    -display none \
    -drive file=tail_disk.img,format=raw,if=sd \
    -netdev user,id=tailnet0 \
    -device usb-net,netdev=tailnet0
```

`tail_qemu.rfs` is a custom ELF container that bundles the entire OS, 16 components:

```
tail_qemu.rfs
├── aarch64-startup                Early boot (EL3 -> EL1, MMU, jump to kernel)
├── kernel                         Microkernel (process, thread, IPC, scheduler)
├── uart_pl011                     UART + TTY server (user-space)
├── gpio_rpi3                      GPIO controller driver
├── sd_sdhost_rpi3                 SD card block driver (user-space)
├── fat_file_system_server         Mounts tail_disk.img as "/"
├── read_only_file_system_server   Serves these files at /rfs
├── log_server                     System log
├── logview                        Copies logged errors to the console
├── pipe_server                    Pipes between processes
├── dwc2_rpi3                      USB host controller driver
├── network                        Network stack
├── netdev_lo_module               Loopback network device
├── route                          Sets the default route at boot
├── debug_server                   GDB remote protocol stub (packed, not started)
└── tsh                            Shell
```

`ls /rfs` lists them, and the shell itself is `/rfs/tsh`. `/rfs` does not appear in
`ls /`, because `ls /` lists the root directory of the FAT disk, and `/rfs` is a separate
file system mounted beside it rather than a directory on that disk. Paths under it work:
`which tsh` prints `/rfs/tsh`.

`tail_disk.img` is exposed to the guest as an SD card. It has two FAT32 partitions, laid
out like the Raspberry Pi 3 image: the first, 64 MiB, is the boot partition a real Pi
reads its firmware from, and it is empty here, because QEMU loads `tail_qemu.rfs`
directly. The second is mounted as `/` and holds:

```
tail_disk.img
├── /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf     Name lookup
├── /hello.py                        Example Python script
├── /usr/bin/                        27 programs: ls, ps, top, vi, python, ping, ... (*)
└── /usr/lib/python3.14/,
    /usr/lib/python314.zip           Python 3.14 standard library
```

(*) Plus `list-root-long`, a copy of `ls` under a long file name that shows the FAT
server's long-name support, so `ls /usr/bin` lists 28 names.

```
qemu-system-aarch64 -M raspi3b
  |
  v
QEMU loads tail_qemu.rfs at 0x80000 (raspi3b entry point)
  |
  v
TAIL OS startup (aarch64-startup)
  |-- Switch EL3 -> EL1
  |-- Initialize MMU, caches
  |-- Jump to kernel
  v
TAIL OS kernel
  |-- Initialize process/thread/IPC/memory subsystems
  |-- Load user-space servers from RFS
  |-- Mount tail_disk.img as "/" via SD + FAT
  |-- Start tsh shell
  v
/$ _
```

**`qemu-system-aarch64: command not found`:**
Install QEMU with `sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils`.

**No output at all in the QEMU window:**
The launcher passes `-serial mon:stdio` for you. If you're running QEMU by
hand, make sure that flag is present — otherwise UART output goes nowhere
visible.

**Want to force a fresh download:**
Clear the cache: `rm -rf ~/.cache/tailos` and re-run the launcher.

**QEMU boots but hangs before `/$`:**
The FAT filesystem takes several seconds to initialize on first boot; give it
up to a minute. If it never appears, re-download the images (the cached copy
may be corrupted) with `rm -rf ~/.cache/tailos`.

**Exiting:**
Inside QEMU, press **Ctrl-A, then lowercase x** to quit. **Ctrl-A, then lowercase c**
drops into the QEMU monitor (type `quit`). Uppercase X and C do nothing.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
You build the SD card image yourself, from two downloads: the TAIL OS SDK, which holds
the toolchain and the prebuilt operating system, and the Raspberry Pi 3 board support
package (BSP), which holds the board's startup code and drivers as source plus the
script that builds the image. To try TAIL OS without hardware, see
[Running TAIL OS in QEMU](install_qemu.md).

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
| Item | Notes |
|------|-------|
| Raspberry Pi 3B or 3B+ | The 3A+ (512 MB) boots the same image in QEMU but has not yet been booted on a board |
| MicroSD card (8 GB+) | |
| USB-to-TTL serial adapter (3.3V) | For serial console (FTDI, CP2102, etc.) |
| 5V / 2.5A power supply | Official RPi PSU recommended |
| Host Linux machine | For building and flashing |

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
Follow [Installation](install_sdk_public.md). It installs the toolchain and the SDK and
writes `tail-sdk-env.sh`, which the BSP uses to find the SDK.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
2. Download the BSP and build the image
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/bsp-rpi3.zip
curl -fsSLO https://tail-os.com/downloads/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
unzip bsp-rpi3.zip
cd bsp-rpi3
source <install dir>/tail-sdk-env.sh
./make-disk.sh
```

`<install dir>` is the directory you gave the SDK installer. `make-disk.sh` checks that
the BSP matches the installed SDK, builds the board crates against it, and writes
`tailos_sd.img`. A BSP and an SDK are published as a pair: if the check rejects your SDK,
install the SDK from the same day's downloads.

The first run downloads the Raspberry Pi boot firmware, about 3 MB, from the official
`raspberrypi/firmware` repository and caches it in `tools/.firmware_cache`. On a machine
without network access, pass `--firmware-dir <dir>` pointing at one directory that
already holds `bootcode.bin`, `start.elf`, `fixup.dat`, `bcm2710-rpi-3-b.dtb`,
`bcm2710-rpi-3-b-plus.dtb` and `miniuart-bt.dtbo`, all side by side. They come from
https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware/tree/master/boot, where `miniuart-bt.dtbo` is
under `overlays/`.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
Replace `/dev/sdX` with your SD card's device:

```bash
sudo dd if=tailos_sd.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress
sync
```

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
Connect the USB-to-TTL serial adapter to the RPi3 GPIO header:

```
USB-TTL Adapter          RPi3 GPIO Header
+-----------+            +----------------+
|           |            |                |
|  TX  o----+----------->| Pin 10 (RXD)  |  GPIO 15
|           |            |                |
|  RX  o<---+-----------o| Pin 8  (TXD)  |  GPIO 14
|           |            |                |
|  GND o----+----------->| Pin 6  (GND)  |
|           |            |                |
+-----------+            +----------------+
```

**Important:** Do NOT connect the VCC/5V pin from the serial adapter to the RPi.
Power the RPi from its own power supply.

Open the serial terminal on your host:

```bash
screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200
# or
minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 115200
```

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
Insert the SD card and power on. The boot log appears on the serial console, and the
shell prompt `/$` follows it.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
Try the image in QEMU first
chunks.text:
The same image boots in QEMU. QEMU does not emulate the Pi's firmware boot chain, so it
loads the operating system from `images/tail.rfs` and takes the SD card image only for
its data partition:

```bash
qemu-system-aarch64 -M raspi3b -kernel images/tail.rfs -serial mon:stdio \
    -display none -drive file=tailos_sd.img,format=raw,if=sd
```

Under QEMU the boot log shows four messages that are not faults. QEMU has no Bluetooth
controller, and the command attaches no USB device, so there is no USB network adapter
to route through:

```
route: the stack refused 10.0.2.2 on netdev_usb0: InvalidInput
[FAIL] usb      no device on the root port
[FAIL] bluetoot bt: opcode 0x0c03 — 0 bytes from controller (unpowered / not routed / wrong baud?)
[FAIL] bt       startup failed: TimedOut
```

Each `[FAIL]` line starts with a timestamp. Their order varies from run to run, and one
can print just after the `/$` prompt; press Enter for a fresh prompt. This image needs a
machine with at least 2 CPUs under QEMU: with one, the boot stops at
`boot waitfor timeout: prefix '/rfs'`.

Exit with **Ctrl-A, then lowercase x**.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
Put a program in `app/<name>/src/main.rs` and add a line `/usr/bin/<name>=<name>` to the
`[disk]` section of `tail.build`. `./make-disk.sh` builds it against the SDK and puts it
in `/usr/bin` on the image. This is also how a program uses the
[Periodic Framework](../framework/periodic/doc/periodic_framework_public.md).

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
```
bsp-rpi3/
├── make-disk.sh       Builds tailos_sd.img (runs the two scripts below)
├── verify-sdk.sh      Checks that the installed SDK matches this BSP
├── build-os.sh        Builds the operating system image, images/tail.rfs
├── bsp.toml           Board manifest: board paths and the SDK this BSP pairs with
├── tail.build         Image manifest: what boots, what starts, what goes on the disk
├── app/build.sh       Builds your programs under app/
├── tools/             SD card image tools (Python 3 standard library only)
├── startup/           Board startup (EL3 to EL1, MMU, jump to the kernel)
├── library/hardware/  Board memory map, power and mailbox crates
└── driver/hardware/   GPIO, SD card (SDHOST and EMMC) and Bluetooth drivers
```

The source is TAIL OS software under licence; see the
[License Guide](license_guide_public.md). The Bluetooth driver includes Broadcom's
firmware for the Pi 3B+ controller, under Broadcom's own licence beside it.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
`make-disk.sh` produces `tailos_sd.img` with the following layout:

```
+===========================================================================+
|                          tailos_sd.img (256 MiB)                          |
+===========================================================================+
|                                                                           |
|  Sector 0: MBR (Master Boot Record)                                       |
|    Partition 1: Boot  | FAT32 | 64 MiB, starting at 1 MiB                 |
|    Partition 2: Data  | FAT32 | 128 MiB                                   |
|    The rest is padding: QEMU's SD emulation needs a power-of-two size.    |
|                                                                           |
|  Partition 1: BOOT                                                        |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+|
|  |  bootcode.bin .... RPi GPU 1st-stage bootloader                       ||
|  |  start.elf ....... RPi GPU firmware                                   ||
|  |  fixup.dat ....... RPi GPU memory fixup                               ||
|  |  bcm2710-rpi-3-b.dtb, bcm2710-rpi-3-b-plus.dtb .. device trees        ||
|  |  overlays/miniuart-bt.dtbo ... routes Bluetooth to the mini-UART      ||
|  |  config.txt ...... Boot configuration (see below)                     ||
|  |  kernel8.img .... TAIL OS (startup + kernel + drivers + servers + tsh)||
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+|
|                                                                           |
|  Partition 2: DATA (mounted as /)                                         |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+|
|  |  /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf .. name lookup                          ||
|  |  /usr/bin/ ...... 26 programs (ls, ps, top, vi, ping, wifi, ...) (*)  ||
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+|
|                                                                           |
+===========================================================================+
```

(*) Plus `list-root-long`, a copy of `ls` under a long file name that shows the FAT
server's long-name support, so `ls /usr/bin` lists 27 names.

Python is not on this image. It comes only with the QEMU download, `tail_disk.img`.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
```
Power On
  |
  v
GPU ROM -> loads bootcode.bin from boot partition
  |
  v
bootcode.bin -> loads start.elf
  |
  v
start.elf -> reads config.txt, loads kernel8.img at 0x80000
  |
  v
TAIL OS startup (aarch64-startup)
  |-- Switch EL3 -> EL1
  |-- Initialize MMU and caches
  |-- Jump to kernel
  v
TAIL OS kernel
  |-- Initialize process/thread/IPC subsystem
  |-- Load drivers and servers from the image (UART, GPIO, SD, Bluetooth, network)
  |-- Mount the data partition via the SD driver + FAT server
  |-- Start tsh shell
  v
/$ _   (serial console ready)
```

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
`make-disk.sh` writes this `config.txt`:

| Setting | Value | Purpose |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `arm_64bit` | `1` | Boot in AArch64 mode |
| `kernel` | `kernel8.img` | Kernel filename to load |
| `disable_commandline_tags` | `1` | Don't pass ATAGS (TAIL OS doesn't use them) |
| `gpu_mem` | `64` | The firmware default. `16` would make the firmware look for a cut-down `start_cd.elf` that is not on the card, and the Pi would not boot |
| `enable_uart` | `1` | Enable serial console |
| `uart_2ndstage` | `1` | Print the firmware's own boot messages on the serial console |
| `dtoverlay` | `miniuart-bt` | Route the onboard Bluetooth controller to the mini-UART and keep it powered |
| `core_freq` | `250` | Pin the core clock so the mini-UART's baud rate stays stable |
| `gpio` | `40,41=ip` | Make GPIO 40/41 inputs. The firmware otherwise routes PWM0/PWM1 to the audio jack on those pins, and TAIL OS drives the same two channels out on GPIO 18/19, so the jack would carry every motor and step pulse too |

TAIL OS's console is the PL011 UART at address `0x3F201000`. TAIL OS's startup code
connects GPIO 14/15 to the PL011 itself, so the console reaches the header pins while
Bluetooth uses the mini-UART.

headingPath: Installing TAIL OS on Raspberry Pi 3
chunks.text:
**No serial output:**
- Verify TX/RX wiring (they must be crossed: adapter TX -> RPi RX)
- Ensure baud rate is 115200
- Check that the SD card's `config.txt` has `enable_uart=1`

**RPi power LED on but no activity LED blinking:**
- The SD card may not be readable. Re-flash with `dd` and verify the boot partition
  contains `bootcode.bin`, `start.elf`, and `kernel8.img`

**`make-disk.sh` rejects the SDK:**
- The BSP was packaged against a different SDK. Install the SDK published with this
  BSP, then run `./make-disk.sh` again.

**Kernel panic or hang after startup:**
- Boot the same image in QEMU first (see above) to see whether the fault depends on
  the hardware, and compare with [Running TAIL OS in QEMU](install_qemu.md)
